# Bootable

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/index.html

A simple, **unopinionated** framework for booting Kotlin applications. It handles starting, stopping, lifecycle management, logging, configuration, and other basic reusable components, and then gets out of your way.

Bootable’s core is plain Kotlin and embeds **no** dependency-injection framework. Its runtime takes two sets, your application services and your lifecycle controllers, and runs them. How you assemble those sets is your choice: wire them by hand, use Bootable’s optional Kodein, Koin, Metro, or Inara bindings, or bring your own DI.

Coming from Spring Boot? See [Bootable and Spring Boot](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/comparison/spring-boot.html.md) for how the two differ, and when each fits.

## Get started

Pick a wiring style. Every page on this site shows its code in the style you pick, and remembers it.

- [Vanilla](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md) Plain Kotlin, no DI framework.
- [Kodein](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md) A runtime DI with a clean DSL; deprecated: consider Inara or Koin.
- [Koin](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md) A runtime DI with a DSL like Kodein’s.
- [Metro](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md) A compile-time DI that checks the graph as it builds.
- [Inara](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md) Kodein’s compile-time successor, checked by KSP; experimental.

## Functions

- [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md) Typed config from HOCON and the environment, with secrets masked.
- [Environment](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/environment/index.html.md) The deployment environment, such as dev or prod, from config.
- [Logging](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md) Log4j2, with plain, coloured, JSON, and Google Cloud output.
- [Database](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/index.html.md) A lifecycle-managed connection pool, migrations, and Exposed.
- [Web / HTTP](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/index.html.md) A Ktor server and clients, with liveness and readiness probes.
- [Background work](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/index.html.md) Periodic loops, leader election, and persistent scheduled tasks.
- [Telemetry](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md) OpenTelemetry traces and metrics, pushed or pulled.
- [Testing](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/testing/index.html.md) Helpers for fast unit tests, with no application booted.

## Examples

Runnable applications that put these functions together; see [Examples](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/index.html.md).

## For LLMs

Each page is also published as Markdown, at its URL with `.md` appended, and [llms.txt](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/llms.txt) indexes them, as [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) describes. [llms-full.txt](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/llms-full.txt) has every page in one file.

# Choosing a wiring style

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html

Bootable’s core embeds no DI framework. Each module ships its plain artifact, and, where it has bindings for them, `-kodein`, `-koin`, `-metro`, and `-inara` artifacts too. Depend on the flavour you wire with.

*Vanilla (no DI)*

Small or single-module apps, or anyone who dislikes DI frameworks. You list your services explicitly. No extra dependencies, no annotations, no compiler plugin.

*Kodein-DI (runtime, deprecated)*

You want multibinding aggregation across modules without a compiler plugin. Kodein is an ordinary jar; wiring is runtime code.

> **Warning:** Kodein is deprecated: its authors are sunsetting it. Consider Inara, its compile-time successor, or, to stick with a style more like Kodein’s, Koin. Bootable’s Kodein bindings are deprecated too.

*Koin (runtime)*

You want a runtime DSL like Kodein’s, from an actively maintained library. Koin is an ordinary jar; wiring is runtime code. Koin has no set multibindings: Bootable collects every definition of a type, such as each `AppService`, and you give each of yours a qualifier of its own.

*Metro (compile-time)*

You want the wiring validated by the compiler: missing and duplicate bindings are build errors, with no runtime reflection. Metro is a Kotlin compiler plugin: it needs Kotlin 2.3 or later, and its Gradle plugin.

*Inara (compile-time, experimental)*

Explicit wiring, checked by the compiler. Inara uses modules declared as interfaces coupled with a simple Kotlin DSL, rather than annotations like Metro. Inara requires KSP; a service is a module member marked `@AppServices`, rather than a multibinding. Bootable’s Inara bindings are experimental, as Inara itself is.

The code on every page comes in a tab per style. The style you choose here, in the header’s **Wiring** switch, or in any tab, shows on every page of the site, and is remembered on your next visit.

---

# All modules

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/modules.html

> Every Bootable module, by function.

Every module Bootable publishes, by function. Within a function, each group’s heading says how to pick from it: choose one, or optional, both of which are dependencies you add, or comes with another module, which you don’t add yourself. A module marked `(-otel)` has an `-otel` variant: the same module, with its telemetry added, which you use in its place. A module with `-kodein`, `-koin`, `-metro`, or `-inara` flavours is installed in the flavour of your wiring style; see [Choosing a wiring style](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md).

## Core

| Module | What it provides |
| --- | --- |
| `boot` | `Bootable`: the application’s services and lifecycle controllers, run phase by phase, and `Health` |
| `boot-common` | Small helpers the other modules share |

# Faster start: the JVM AOT cache

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/aot-cache.html

> Start a Bootable application faster from a JVM AOT cache, trained by a Gradle task, in a Jib image, or in a Dagger pipeline.

On JDK 24 and later, an AOT cache ([JEP 483](https://openjdk.org/jeps/483), with the one-step training of [JEP 514](https://openjdk.org/jeps/514) in JDK 25) holds the classes an application loaded and linked during a training run, so the next start reads them from the cache instead of loading, verifying and linking them again. A Bootable application’s start loads thousands of classes, from Log4j, Hoplite, the database and telemetry libraries, and Ktor, so it gains a lot from one. See Spring’s [guide to the AOT cache](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/integration/aot-cache.html) for more on how it works.

## Producing the cache

The training run starts the application with `-XX:AOTCacheOutput=<file>`, and the JVM writes the cache when the application exits. The `bootable.aot-cache` plugin in [build-logic](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/build-logic) adds an `aotCache` task to an application, which does that with the installed distribution (`installDist`), by its start script, on the project’s Java toolchain:

- it starts the application, and waits for Bootable’s `=> Running` line, which it logs once every service has started;
- it sends the application the requests given to it, if any, so the cache also covers the request path, not just the start;
- it stops the application with SIGTERM, so it shuts down as it would in production, and the JVM writes the cache as it exits.

```kotlin
plugins {
  application
  id("bootable.aot-cache")
}

tasks.aotCache {
  environment.put("SERVER_HOSTPORT", "127.0.0.1:18001")
  request("PUT", "http://127.0.0.1:18001/entries/trained", "by the AOT training run")
  request("GET", "http://127.0.0.1:18001/entries/trained")
  rounds = 20
}
```

Train with the configuration the application runs with in production, as the cache only holds the classes the training loaded. Telemetry is the usual difference: with an OTLP endpoint, the OpenTelemetry SDK builds its OTLP exporters, and loads about 760 classes that a training run without one leaves out of the cache. So the examples' training runs set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` to an address nothing listens on: the training exports nothing, and logs a failed export as it stops. The Jib image below, started with an endpoint, loaded 914 classes from outside a cache trained without one, and 144 from outside one trained with one, as many as it does without an endpoint.

The plugin is one file, `AotCache.kt`, with no dependencies but Gradle’s own, so an application outside this repository can copy it into its own `buildSrc` or build logic. The task type, `AotCacheTraining`, runs any command that starts the application with `-XX:AOTCacheOutput`, such as a container, as the Jib example below does. The training needs a JVM that writes the cache as it exits, on SIGTERM, so it runs on Linux and macOS, not Windows.

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:vanilla:aotCache
```

writes `examples/server-ktor-db/vanilla/build/aot/vanilla.aot`, and the application’s output during the training next to it, in `vanilla.aot.log`. The cache is about 66 MB for that example, or 60 MB for a training run that only starts it.

## Running with the cache

Run the application with `-XX:AOTCache=<file>`, on the same JDK, from the same installed directory:

```shell
cd examples/server-ktor-db/vanilla
JAVA_OPTS=-XX:AOTCache=build/aot/vanilla.aot build/install/vanilla/bin/vanilla
```

The JVM only uses the cache with the JDK build that wrote it, and the same class path, of the same jars, which it checks by their sizes and modification times. On any difference, it warns, such as `The AOT cache was created by a different version or build of HotSpot`, or `This file is not the one used while building the AOT cache`, and runs without the cache. So train with the application as it ships, and ship them together:

- the installed directory can move, but a copy of it has to keep the files' modification times, as `cp -a`, `rsync -a` or a tar archive of it do; a rerun of `installDist` writes new ones, so `aotCache` runs again after it;
- in a container image, train in a container of the image itself, as the Jib example below does.

`-XX:AOTMode=on` makes the JVM fail to start rather than run without the cache, which shows a mismatch at once. `-Xlog:aot` logs whether the JVM opened the cache, and `-Xlog:class+load` logs each class that came from it with `source: shared objects file`.

## The gain

On the vanilla [examples/server-ktor-db](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/server-ktor-db) app, on JDK 25, the median of 7 starts:

|  | Without the cache | With the cache |
| --- | --- | --- |
| From launch to `=> Running` | 721 ms | 307 ms |
| From `boot` to `=> Running` | 690 ms | 229 ms |
| From `boot` to the services starting | 485 ms | 160 ms |
| The first `PUT /entries/{name}` | 44 ms | 12 ms |

The cache held 8,217 of the 8,368 classes the application loaded through its start and those first requests. A cache from a training run that only starts the application starts it as fast, but leaves the first request at 47 ms: the training’s requests are what cover the request path.

## In a container image, with Jib

[examples/server-ktor-db/jib](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/server-ktor-db/jib) builds the vanilla app into a container image, with [Jib](https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/jib), with its AOT cache in it:

1. `jibBuildTar` builds the image without a cache, and the container runtime loads it;
2. `aotCache` runs that image once, in a container, with `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` in place of the image’s `-XX:AOTCache`, and the cache’s directory mounted from the build, so the training runs on the image’s own JDK, with its class path, `-cp @/app/jib-classpath-file`;
3. `jibDockerBuild`, or `jib` to push to a registry, builds the final image, with the cache as one more layer, at `/app/aot/server-ktor-db.aot`, and `-XX:AOTCache` in its JVM flags.

Jib’s images are reproducible, with every file’s modification time fixed, so the final image’s jars are the same, to the JVM, as those the cache was trained with. Two settings make the cache usable at all: `containerizingMode = "packaged"`, which puts the application’s own classes in a jar, as the JVM won’t use a cache with a non-empty directory on the class path, as Jib’s default `/app/classes` is; and the training’s entrypoint, the image’s own but for the cache’s flag, as the JVM takes only one of `-XX:AOTCache` and `-XX:AOTCacheOutput`.

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:jib:jibDockerBuild -PcontainerCli=podman
podman run --rm -p 8001:8001 bootable-examples/server-ktor-db-jib
```

`containerCli` is the container runtime’s command, for loading and running the training image and for `jibDockerBuild`: `docker` by default, or `podman`. The cache adds a 68 MB layer to the image, which used 9,406 of the 9,550 classes the application had loaded once it was running, and started from launch to `=> Running` in a median of 399 ms with the cache, and 896 ms without it, over 7 starts, each in a new container. With an OTLP endpoint, it started in 400 ms with the cache, as `boot-telemetry-otel` creates the exporters' HTTP clients on their first export, after the start.

The JVM’s choice of garbage collector, and so part of what the cache holds, depends on the container’s memory and CPUs: train with the same limits the application runs with.

## In a CI pipeline, with Dagger

The `server-ktor-db` [Dagger](https://dagger.io) module, in `.dagger/modules/server-ktor-db/main.dang`, builds the Jib image above with its cache as a CI pipeline, in containers, with nothing on the host but the `dagger` CLI and a container runtime. It is written in [Dang](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang), Dagger’s own language, and needs the Dagger 1.0 beta. It is one file, with no generated code and no package manager.

Dagger needs a container runtime: Docker, or Podman with its socket enabled. `mise install` provides the Dagger CLI. The module needs the 1.0 beta, which the stable CLI downloads and runs when `DAGGER_X_RELEASE` names it; `mise.toml` sets that variable. Without mise, install a stable CLI of 0.21.3 or later, and export `DAGGER_X_RELEASE=v1.0.0-beta.28`. Bootable sends no traces to Dagger Cloud unless you provide your own `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN` or run `dagger login`.

```bash
dagger check
dagger api call server-ktor-db image export --path=build/server-ktor-db.tar
podman load -i build/server-ktor-db.tar
```

`dagger check` runs every function marked `@check`, which here is `check`. The other functions are called by name, as `dagger api call server-ktor-db <function>`.

| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `check` | The pull request check: builds the image, and runs `verify`. Publishes nothing. |
| `jib-image` | The Jib image, without a cache, as a tarball, from Gradle’s `jibBuildTar`, built in `eclipse-temurin:25-jdk`, with Gradle’s user home, and its build cache, and Jib’s base image cache, in cache volumes. |
| `runtime` | `jib-image`, imported as a container. |
| `aot-cache` | The cache, from a training run of `runtime`: the app started as the image’s entrypoint does, but with `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` in place of its `-XX:AOTCache`, then `=> Running`, the training requests, and SIGTERM. `--requests` and `--rounds` change the requests. |
| `image` | `runtime`, with the cache where its entrypoint’s `-XX:AOTCache` looks for it, at `/app/aot/server-ktor-db.aot`. `image export --path=<file>.tar` writes it to disk. |
| `verify` | Starts `image`, and fails unless at least `--min-percent`, by default 90, of the classes it loads come from the cache. `verify stdout` says how many. |
| `env` | The build container before Gradle has run. `dagger api call server-ktor-db env terminal` opens a shell in it. |
| `dev` | `image`, on port 8001, exporting its traces and metrics over OTLP to the module’s `collector` setting, which `dagger.toml` wires to the `otel-lgtm` module’s `otel-stack`. `--tracing=false` exports nothing, and starts no collector. |

The `otel-lgtm` module, in `.dagger/modules/otel-lgtm/main.dang`, runs Grafana’s `otel-lgtm` stack, to demo the traces and metrics: an OpenTelemetry collector, Prometheus, Tempo, Loki and Grafana, in one container. It isn’t part of Bootable, so it is a module of its own, and `dagger.toml` wires its `otel-stack` into `server-ktor-db`'s `collector` setting, as `dag://otel-lgtm/otel-stack`. `mise.toml` has a task for each way to run the example, each on port 8001:

| Task | What it runs |
| --- | --- |
| `mise run demo` | `dagger start server-ktor-db/dev otel-lgtm/otel-stack`: the app, exporting to the stack, and the stack, tunneling the app’s port, 8001, Grafana’s, 3000, and the collector’s, 4318, to `localhost`. |
| `mise run demo-without-tracing` | `dagger api call server-ktor-db dev --tracing=false up`: the app alone, exporting nothing. `dagger start` can’t pass a function’s arguments, so this calls `dev` with `--tracing=false`, and `up` tunnels its port. |

`dagger start` doesn’t show the services' own output, such as the app’s log: its view shows only the tunnels and the ports' health checks. `dagger start --progress logs` prints it, under the function that defines each service, such as `ServerKtorDb.dev`, and `mise run demo — --progress logs` passes the flag on.

Jib builds the image, without a container runtime, and the module trains the cache in a container of it, then adds the cache to that same container, so the JDK build, and the jars' sizes and modification times, are the training’s by construction. The image is defined once, in the Jib example’s build, for both Gradle and Dagger: its base image, JVM flags, class path, port and environment. The Jib build pins its base image, the JRE, by digest, so the JDK build only changes when the digest does, and the cache is trained again with it; `dagger.lock` pins the build’s JDK image.

Dagger sets `OTEL_*` variables in every container, for its own tracing, and forwards what they collect to Dagger Cloud when the CLI is logged in to it. The module unsets them before it starts the app, which would otherwise export its own telemetry there, and sets an OTLP endpoint of its own, on the container’s localhost, where nothing listens, so the cache has the OTLP exporters' classes, as in the Gradle examples.

Its image used 9,404 of the 9,561 classes it loaded from its cache, and started from launch to `=> Running` in a median of 386 ms with the cache, and 900 ms without it, over 7 starts, each in a new container.

## Which to use

- The `aotCache` task, for an application shipped as its installed distribution, or to try the cache locally: it trains on the build’s own JDK toolchain, and needs nothing else.
- Jib, for a container image built by Gradle, without a Dockerfile: the training needs a container runtime, to run the image once.
- Dagger, for a CI pipeline that runs the same way on a laptop and on any CI service, where the build, the training and the image are each a cached, containerized step: it builds the same Jib image, so the host needs only Dagger and a container runtime, not a JDK, and the training runs on the image’s own JDK by construction.

---

# Concepts

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/index.html

> The ideas the rest of the site builds on: Bootable's approach, the application's lifecycle, and the order services start in.

A few ideas run through every function’s page. Read these first, and the rest of the site makes sense.

**[No magic](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/philosophy.html.md)**

Bootable boots and runs your application, and nothing more: no scanning, no auto-configuration, no embedded DI, and typed config. What it deliberately leaves out, and why.

**[Lifecycle and services](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html.md)**

An application is a set of services, which lifecycle controllers start and stop. How `boot` builds and runs it, its states, what happens when a start fails, and how it shuts down.

**[Start order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md)**

The order the services start in: phases, milestones within a phase, the tiebreaker for the rest, and how an application changes the order.

---

# No magic

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/philosophy.html

> Bootable is a simple, unopinionated framework for booting and running applications: explicit wiring, typed config, and the libraries underneath used directly.

Bootable is a simple, unopinionated framework for booting and running applications. Your `main` builds the application, from objects you construct or your DI constructs, and hands it to Bootable, which starts it, runs it, and stops it. Nothing happens that the code doesn’t say.

An important element of simplicity is to prefer explicit references and configuration. Spring Boot discovers and configures components at runtime, through annotations and reflection, which is easy, but not simple: to use it, you have to understand the libraries underneath, and Spring Boot’s own annotations and library abstractions on top. Bootable aims to be both [easy and simple](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/Simple-Made-Easy/): a minimal core that runs your application, and modules that integrate common, useful libraries for server-side applications. It provides your application with comprehensive lifecycle control, and includes some optional batteries for common functionality, and then gets out of your way. [Bootable and Spring Boot](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/comparison/spring-boot.html.md) compares the two in more detail.

## Two sets, run

Bootable’s core, `Bootable`, takes two sets: your application’s services, and its lifecycle controllers. It starts the services in order, runs until it is asked to stop, and stops them in reverse. See [Lifecycle and services](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html.md) for more detail.

That is all the core does. In particular, it has:

**No classpath scanning**

Bootable never looks for classes to instantiate. A service runs because it is in the set you pass.

**No annotations that change behaviour**

Nothing in Bootable reads an annotation at runtime. Metro’s annotations, if you wire with Metro, describe the dependency graph and nothing else: they don’t make a method transactional, or a class a service.

**No auto-configuration**

A Bootable module does nothing until you wire it: you construct its service, or import its DI module. The one place a dependency alone adds to the application is Metro’s discovery, which you turn on in your graph, with `additionalScopes = [BootScope::class]`, and which the compiler checks; an explicit graph names every container instead.

**No embedded DI framework**

The core is plain Kotlin, and `Bootable` takes its two sets through an ordinary constructor.

## Your wiring, your choice

How you assemble the two sets is up to you. Wire them by hand, with Kodein, with Koin, with Metro, with Inara, or with any other DI, such as a service loader or Guice.

For convenience, each module that has something to wire ships optional bindings, as separate `-kodein`, `-koin`, `-metro`, and experimental `-inara` artifacts. Each depends on the plain module, so the flavour you depend on is all you choose, module by module. Every page on this site shows its code in each of the five styles; [Choosing a wiring style](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md) helps you pick one.

A small application can list its services by hand. As it grows into modules, each with services that no central code knows about, collecting them into a set is what a DI container’s multibindings do well. For most teams, the authors of Bootable recommend Metro, though Bootable itself has no opinion, which builds and checks the graph at compile time, so a missing binding is a build error rather than a failed start. Kodein has no compile-time checking, and builds the graph at runtime, but its DSL is short and readable; its authors are sunsetting it, so Bootable’s Kodein bindings are deprecated. Inara, Kodein’s compile-time successor from the same authors, is experimental. Koin, like Kodein, builds the graph at runtime, with a DSL much like Kodein’s.

## Typed config, no hidden defaults

Each module reads its config into a typed class, from a section you name when you bind it, such as `db.pool` for the connection pool. A setting’s default is the default of the class’s property, in the code and in its API reference, so what an unset key means is never somewhere else. Config that doesn’t decode fails the start before any service starts.

Bootable doesn’t load per-environment files, such as `application-prod.conf`, chosen by a variable outside the config. A mistyped environment would silently load nothing, and the config would no longer say where a value came from. An application that wants such files adds them to its binder explicitly. See [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md).

## What Bootable doesn’t do

Bootable provides useful capabilities on top of well-chosen libraries, not an abstraction over them. It deliberately leaves these out:

**Interchangeable libraries**

Bootable doesn’t make the libraries it builds on, such as Hoplite for configuration, or Exposed and HikariCP for databases, interchangeable with others. You use their types and APIs directly, and Bootable exposes them rather than wrapping them. The same goes for DI: Bootable provides bindings for Kodein, Koin, Metro, and Inara, not an abstraction over them.

**Every feature of every library**

Bootable’s modules set up the common case. For anything more, you configure the library itself, through the hooks a module provides, such as a `HikariConfigCustomizer`, or skip Bootable’s module entirely and bring your own code.

**Requiring Bootable’s modules**

You can use Bootable’s modules, integrate a library yourself, or use a different library that fits better. Bootable’s core is application lifecycle management; every other module is optional.

**Booting the application in tests**

Bootable won’t add a way to boot the application in a test. Where one exists, it tends to become the way every test is written, because nobody then has to think about fakes, and the tests become slow and brittle. Construct a class with fakes for what it uses, and check the wiring, and the start plan, without starting anything; see [Testing](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/testing/index.html.md).

Contrast this with Spring Boot, which tends to put its own factories and APIs in front of the underlying libraries. That moves the understanding you need from the library to Spring’s abstraction over it. It also makes the unique capabilities of the libraries you use harder, or even impossible, to reach.

---

# Lifecycle and services

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html

> How Bootable builds, starts, runs, and stops an application: services, lifecycle controllers, states, start failures, and shutdown.

An application is a set of services, each with a start and a stop, and a set of lifecycle controllers, which decide when the services start and stop. `boot` builds the application, and `Bootable` runs it: it starts the services in their [start order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md), waits until it is asked to stop, and stops them in reverse.

## The application

An application’s `main` calls `boot { }`, whose block builds the application and returns a `Bootable`. Here, an application with one service, `HelloServer`, a [Ktor server](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md) that answers `hello` on port 8000:

**Vanilla:**

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  Bootable(setOf(HelloServer(HostPort(port = 8000))))
}
```

**Kodein:**

`bootableModule` binds `Bootable`, and opens the sets; `bindAppService` adds a service to them:

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  val di = DI {
    import(bootableModule)       // Bootable, its default controllers, and the sets to contribute into
    bindAppService { singleton { HelloServer(HostPort(port = 8000)) } }
  }
  di.direct.instance<Bootable>()
}
```

**Koin:**

`bootableModule()` defines `Bootable`, over every `AppService` and `LifecycleController` definition; give each of yours a qualifier of its own:

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  val koin = koinApplication {
    modules(
      bootableModule(),  // Bootable, its default controllers, and every AppService and LifecycleController definition
      module { single<AppService>(named<HelloServer>()) { HelloServer(HostPort(port = 8000)) } },
    )
  }.koin
  koin.get<Bootable>()
}
```

**Metro:**

A service contributed into the `Set<AppService>` is in the application; scope it with `@SingleIn`, so the instance that runs is the only one:

```kotlin
@ContributesTo(AppScope::class)
interface HelloBindings {
  @Provides @IntoSet @SingleIn(AppScope::class)
  fun server(): AppService = HelloServer(HostPort(port = 8000))
}

// BootableGraph brings Bootable, its default controllers, and the sets to contribute into
@DependencyGraph(AppScope::class, additionalScopes = [BootScope::class])
interface AppGraph : BootableGraph

fun main() = boot {
  createGraph<AppGraph>().bootable
}
```

**Inara:**

The application’s module is composed of Bootable’s, whose `bootable` runs every member marked `@AppServices`; `BootableModule` requires a `ConfigModule`, here `EmptyConfigModule`, for an application without config:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface AppModule : ConfigModule, BootableModule {
  @AppServices val helloServer: HelloServer
}

fun main() = boot {
  AppModule(
    configModule = EmptyConfigModule,   // no config: Bootable's defaults
    bootableModule = bootableModule(),  // Bootable, its default controllers, and the sets to mark members into
    helloServer = Binding.single { HelloServer(HostPort(port = 8000)) },
  ).bootable
}
```

`boot` initializes logging and then delegates to the passed block to return a `Bootable` with the application’s services and lifecycle controllers (or defaults) injected. `boot` then runs the `Bootable` it returned. `Bootable` starts all the registered services and runs until it is told to stop, generally through a process signal or other internal or external shutdown signal, and then shuts down services cleanly and exits the process with the application’s exit code.

Both [`boot`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/boot.html) and [`Bootable`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-bootable/index.html) take optional parameters for additional control over logging, shutdown, and lifecycle.

`boot` runs the application on the main thread, in `runBlocking`. What it calls, `Bootable`'s `run`, is a suspending function that returns the exit code rather than exiting, so a test, or a host that embeds an application, can run one in a coroutine, and stop it with `Bootable`'s `stop`.

## Services

A service is anything with a lifecycle: a connection pool, a server, a background loop. It implements `AppService`, as `HelloServer` does, which runs a Ktor server while the application runs:

```kotlin
class HelloServer(private val config: HostPort) : AppService {
  private lateinit var server: EmbeddedServer<*, *>

  override suspend fun start() {
    server = embeddedServer(CIO, port = config.port(8080)) {
      routing {
        get("/") { call.respondText("hello") }
      }
    }
    server.startSuspend()
  }

  override suspend fun shutdown() {
    server.stopSuspend(gracePeriodMillis = 50, timeoutMillis = 1_000)
  }

  override fun ordering() = Ordering(DefaultPhase.Serving)
}
```

**`start`**

Acquires what the service runs with, and returns once it is running. Here, it binds the port and starts the engine. Services start one at a time, so a `start` that takes long holds up the rest. A service with background work of its own, such as a loop, overrides `start(scope)` instead, and launches that work in the scope it gets, the service’s own.

**`shutdown`**

Releases it: here, it stops the engine, letting the requests in flight finish. It is called only if `start` returned. A service needn’t stop what it launched in its scope: once `shutdown` returns, Bootable cancels the scope, and waits for its coroutines.

**`ordering`**

Where the service starts, relative to the others; see [Start order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md). A server starts in the `Serving` phase, once the services it uses have started, and stops first. The default suits most of an application’s own services.

**`name`**

The service’s name in the logs and the start plan, its class’s simple name by default.

Constructing a service and starting it are separate steps. The constructor takes what the service uses, and does nothing with it; `start` opens connections, binds ports, and starts threads. So building the application has no side effects: a test can construct it, and check its wiring and its start plan, without starting anything.

An application needn’t write a server this way: [`boot-server-http-ktor`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md)'s `CioKtorService` and `NettyKtorService` do all of this, so a server extends one, and writes only its Ktor module, as the [Ktor server](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor.html.md) example does, on Netty.

`start` and `shutdown` are suspending, and run on the lifecycle’s own thread, the main thread under `boot`, one service at a time. The scope that `start(scope)` gets is a child of the application’s scope, on `Dispatchers.Default`, so the work a service launches there runs on that dispatcher. Wrap blocking calls in them, such as JDBC or file IO, in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)`. Bootable stops a service’s work by cancelling it, so code that catches `Exception` must not swallow a `CancellationException`; the [`AppService`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-app-service/index.html) reference shows how to rethrow it.

A service’s scope is a child of the application’s, so nothing a service launches there outlives the application. Don’t launch background work anywhere else, such as in `GlobalScope`, or a scope the service makes itself: nothing stops that work when the application stops, and its failure doesn’t stop the application.

### When a service fails while it runs

A coroutine that fails in a service’s scope, such as a server whose engine stops, fails the service. Bootable cancels the service’s other coroutines, marks it `Failed`, and stops the application, in order, with exit code 1. A service that notices outside its scope, such as in a request handler, that it can’t go on, fails it with `scope.launch { throw e }`.

The service’s `scopeFailurePolicy` changes that. `ScopeFailurePolicy.StopApplication(exitCode)` stops the application with another exit code. `ScopeFailurePolicy.LogAndContinue` suits a service whose coroutines are independent of each other, such as fire-and-forget work launched from request handlers: a coroutine that fails is logged, and the service and the application carry on.

## Lifecycle controllers

A lifecycle controller decides when services start and stop, and can run code around the application’s lifecycle. `defaultLifecycleControllers()` has three:

**`AppStartStopLifecycleController`**

Starts every service, in the start plan’s order, when the application starts, and stops them in reverse when it shuts down.

**`StopSignalHandlerLifecycleController`**

Shuts the application down on `HUP`, `INT`, or `TERM`, such as Ctrl-C or a container’s stop.

**`HealthLifecycleController`**

Tracks the application’s state, for [liveness and readiness](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md).

A controller implements `LifecycleController`, whose methods all do nothing by default, and those that may do IO suspend:

- `appInit`, before any service starts.
- `appStart`, to start the application, with a callback that stops it later.
- `aroundAppStart`, to run code around the whole start, and `aroundServiceStart`, around each service’s.
- `appRunning`, once the whole start has completed.
- `serviceStartVote`, to keep a service from starting.
- `appShutdown` and `appCleanup`, as the application stops.

A controller’s `priority` orders it against the other controllers; it has nothing to do with the order the services start in, which is the [start plan](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md). A higher priority’s `appInit` and `appStart` run first, its `aroundAppStart` and `aroundServiceStart` are outermost, and its `appShutdown` runs last. `AppStartStopLifecycleController` has the highest priority, so its `appStart` starts the services before any other controller’s runs, and its `appShutdown` stops them after every other controller’s; `HealthLifecycleController` has the lowest, so readiness goes down before anything else stops.

Bootable’s own modules add controllers this way. [`HealthLifecycleController`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md) tracks the application’s state, and waits for load balancers when shutdown begins. [`ServiceStartTracing`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md#start-tracing) traces the start, as a span around the application’s start, from `aroundAppStart`, and one around each service’s, from `aroundServiceStart`.

### Turning services off and on

The default controllers start everything at boot, but that is a choice, not a rule. `appStart` receives the services, and a `serviceStart` and a `serviceShutdown` that start and stop any one of them, at any time while the application runs. Every start, at boot or later, first asks each controller’s `serviceStartVote`, and a service that any controller votes `NO` on doesn’t start.

So a controller of your own can switch services off and on while the process runs: it votes `NO` on the disabled ones, and stops or starts a service as it is disabled or enabled. Which are disabled can come from config that reloads, such as a Kubernetes ConfigMap, or from commands, such as messages on a topic, to stop a queue consumer during maintenance.

## States

The application is in one of four states, which `HealthLifecycleController` tracks:

**`Starting`**

From the start, until the whole start has completed.

**`Running`**

Every service has started, and so has every controller.

**`Stopping`**

Shutdown has begun. A start that fails goes here too.

**`Stopped`**

Every service has stopped.

Liveness and readiness are answered from them: the application is live until it has stopped, and ready only while it is running, and its readiness checks pass. See [Health](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md).

Each service has a state of its own too, a `ServiceState`: `Pending`, `Starting`, `Running`, `Skipped` (a controller voted against its start), `Failed`, `Stopping`, or `Stopped`. Controllers see them in the `ServiceContext`, and the health reports include them.

## The start

`Bootable` logs each step of the start as it goes:

1. `⇒ Creating application`: `boot` runs the passed block, which decodes the config and constructs the services.
2. `Start plan: …​`: it computes the order the services start in, and logs it; see [the start plan](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md#start-plan).
3. `⇒ Initializing`: each controller’s `appInit`.
4. `⇒ Starting`: each controller’s `appStart`, which, for `AppStartStopLifecycleController`, starts each service in turn, logged as `=⇒ Starting HelloServer…`.
5. `⇒ Running`: every service has started, and the signal handlers are installed.

## When the start fails

The application fails as early as it can, and stops what it started:

- Config that doesn’t decode, or a service that can’t be constructed, fails in `boot`'s block, before anything has started.
- A start order that can’t be met fails before any controller runs; see [validation](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md#validation).
- A service whose `start` throws fails the start. The services that had started are stopped, in reverse, and the one that failed isn’t, since its `start` never returned: a service that must release what it acquired before it failed does so in `start`, before it throws.

Either way, the failure is logged, and the process exits with -1.

A stop asked for during the start, such as by a signal, cancels the start, at the starting service’s next suspension point, and the services that had started are stopped.

## Shutdown

The application stops when it is asked to:

- on `HUP`, `INT`, or `TERM`, by `StopSignalHandlerLifecycleController`, with exit code 0;
- when a service fails while it runs, with exit code 1, unless its [`scopeFailurePolicy`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html.md#failure) says otherwise;
- when code calls `Bootable`'s `stop`, with the exit code it gives;
- by a JVM shutdown hook, as a fallback, if the JVM begins to exit while the application runs, which waits for the stop.

The first of these counts, and any after it change nothing. The signal handlers are installed once every service has started; until then, a signal reaches the JVM, whose shutdown hook stops the application.

Shutdown is logged as `⇒ Shutting down`. Readiness goes down first, and `HealthLifecycleController` waits for its [drain delay](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md#drain), if there is one, so load balancers stop routing to the application before its server stops. Then the services stop, in the reverse of the start plan, each logged as `=⇒ Stopping HelloServer…`, so a server stops before what it uses, and the connection pools close once nothing uses them; see [the shutdown order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md#shutdown). A service that throws as it stops is logged, and the rest still stop.

Once a service has stopped, Bootable cancels its scope, and waits for its coroutines.

The services have `maxShutdownTime`, 30 seconds by default, to stop. After that, Bootable cancels the stop: the service stopping is cancelled, and those not yet stopped are skipped. It logs each service’s state, the coroutines still running, and the threads' stacks, to show what is stuck, and exits with exit code 1. A service blocked in code that ignores cancellation, such as a blocking call, doesn’t return when it is cancelled, so if the stop still hasn’t returned 5 seconds later, Bootable halts the process. The drain delay comes before this timeout starts, so a platform’s grace period, such as Kubernetes’s `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, must cover both.

When every service has stopped, it logs `⇒ Stopped`, and the process exits.

## Reference

- [`boot`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/boot.html): the entry point
- [`Bootable`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-bootable/index.html): the runtime
- [`AppService`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-app-service/index.html): a service
- [`ScopeFailurePolicy`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-scope-failure-policy/index.html): what a failure in a service’s scope does
- [`LifecycleController`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-lifecycle-controller/index.html): a controller
- [`AppStartStopLifecycleController`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-app-start-stop-lifecycle-controller/index.html), [`StopSignalHandlerLifecycleController`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-stop-signal-handler-lifecycle-controller/index.html), and [`HealthLifecycleController`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-health-lifecycle-controller/index.html): the default controllers
- [`LifecycleState`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-lifecycle-state/index.html) and [`ServiceState`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-service-state/index.html): the states

---

# Start order

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html

> How Bootable orders services: phases, milestones within a phase, the tiebreaker, the logged start plan, and custom start orders.

Services start phase by phase, and, within a phase, after the services that provide the milestones they wait for. Services that neither orders are tied, and a tiebreaker orders them. They stop in exactly the reverse order.

Each service says where it starts with its `ordering()`, an `Ordering` of its phase and its milestones. Bootable computes the order, the _start plan_, from the set of services it is given, before anything starts, and logs it. The order is the same whether the services were wired by hand, by Kodein, by Koin, or by Metro, since it comes from the services themselves.

## Phases

Bootable’s default phases, in start order:

| Phase | Holds | Bootable’s modules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Telemetry` | What every other service records into, so it can record from its first moment, and what it records while it stops is still exported. | The OpenTelemetry SDK; the [health probes' own listener](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md#listener), so liveness answers while the others start. |
| `Infrastructure` | Connections to the systems the application needs, and the plumbing the rest relies on. | The [database pool](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/index.html.md), and Exposed’s `Database`; the [HTTP clients](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/client.html.md); [leader election](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md). |
| `Initialization` | Work that brings shared state into shape before the application uses it, such as migrations, schema checks, seed data, and cache warm-up. | [Flyway’s migrations](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/flyway.html.md); Exposed’s [schema verification](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/exposed.html.md). |
| `Application` | The application’s own services: what the work needs, but not what brings the work in. The default phase. | None: this phase is the application’s. |
| `Serving` | Whatever brings work in: HTTP and gRPC servers, queue consumers, schedulers. It starts last, once what it uses is running, and stops first, so work in flight can finish. | The [Ktor server](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md); [periodic work](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html.md); the [db-scheduler](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/scheduler.html.md). |

Most of an application’s services declare no phase, and start in `Application`. A service that brings work in declares `Serving`:

```kotlin
class OrderConsumer : AppService {
  // brings work in, so it starts once everything it uses has, and stops first
  override fun ordering() = Ordering(DefaultPhase.Serving)
}
```

To choose a phase, ask, in this order:

1. Does every other service record into it? `Telemetry`. Applications rarely write one.
2. Does it bring work in? `Serving`, whatever the protocol: a timer firing is work arriving, as a request is.
3. Is it a connection, or plumbing, that others use? `Infrastructure`: the application’s own handle on a system, such as its pool, not the system itself.
4. Does it change or check shared state once, before anyone uses it? `Initialization`.
5. Otherwise, `Application`.

A service that is both used by others and brings work in, such as one that consumes messages, is usually two services: the part others use in `Application`, and the consumer in `Serving`.

The `Initialization` phase isn’t a lifecycle controller’s `appInit`, logged as `⇒ Initializing`, which runs before any service starts; see [the start](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html.md#start).

## Milestones

Within a phase, a milestone orders one service after another. A milestone is a named point that a service reaches once its `start` returns. A service `provides` milestones, and starts `after` the ones it waits for:

```kotlin
object PricingMilestones {
  val RatesLoaded = milestone("pricing.rates.loaded")
}

class ExchangeRates : AppService {
  override suspend fun start() { /* load today's rates */ }
  override fun ordering() = Ordering(provides = setOf(PricingMilestones.RatesLoaded))
}

class PriceCalculator(private val rates: ExchangeRates) : AppService {
  override suspend fun start() { /* compute the prices from the rates */ }
  override fun ordering() = Ordering(after = setOf(PricingMilestones.RatesLoaded))
}
```

A service waits for every provider of a milestone, and a milestone can have several, or none. A provider in an earlier phase has already started, so a milestone matters only between services in the same phase.

A milestone names a role, not a class, so a service orders itself after a role, whichever module fills it. Bootable’s own:

- `DbMilestones.DataSourceReady`, when the connection pool has started, and `DbMilestones.SchemaMigrated`, when the migrations have run: Exposed’s schema verification runs after the migrations without knowing which tool ran them, or whether there is one.
- `HttpClientMilestones.ClientsReady`, when the HTTP clients have started, which leader election waits for.

`Phase` and `Milestone` are interfaces with only a `name`, so an `enum` or an `object` is one with no code; `milestone(name)` makes one that is just a name.

### `after` or `requires`

`after` is the everyday relation: it waits for the providers there are, and is satisfied if there are none. `requires` waits too, but fails the boot if no service provides the milestone:

```kotlin
class ReportService(private val dataSource: DataSource) : AppService {
  // expects the schema to be migrated, by whichever migration tool the application uses
  override fun ordering() = Ordering(requires = setOf(DbMilestones.SchemaMigrated))
}
```

Use `requires` only for a precondition that nothing else enforces. If a service receives what it depends on in its constructor, as `PriceCalculator` does, the wiring already guarantees it exists, and `after` is enough.

## Unordered services

Two services in the same phase, with no milestone between them, are unordered. Bootable may start them in either order, and which it is isn’t part of the contract: if the order matters, a milestone is missing. There is deliberately no priority number to break ties, since a number would be easier to write than the milestone it stands for.

A `StartOrder.Tiebreaker`, given to `Bootable`, decides how ties are broken:

**`ByName`, the default**

By `name()`, so the start plan, and the logs, are the same on every run and every machine.

**`Shuffled`**

At random, from a seed that is logged with the plan, so a missing milestone that a fixed order would hide shows up, and `Shuffled(seed)` replays the order.

Set it in config, in `boot.service.order`:

```hocon
boot.service.order {
  tiebreaker {
    _type = Shuffled  (1)
    seed = 42         (2)
  }
}
```

- (1) `ByName` if unset; `BOOT_SERVICE_ORDER_TIEBREAKER=Shuffled` as an environment variable.
- (2) Optional: replays a logged shuffle; `BOOT_SERVICE_ORDER_TIEBREAKER_SEED=42` as an environment variable.

A good approach is to shuffle in `application-local.conf`, for development, and in the tests' config, where a surprise is cheap, and to keep the default in production, so it starts in the same order on every run. Kodein’s `bootableModule`, Koin’s `bootableModule()`, and Metro’s `BootableDefaultBindings` read the section when there is a `ConfigBinder`; wired by hand, pass `tiebreaker = serviceOrderConfig(binder).tiebreaker` to `Bootable`, as [Custom start orders](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md#custom) shows. A test can check the start plan under many shuffles, without starting anything; see [the start plan](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/testing/index.html.md#start-plans).

## Shutdown order

Services stop in the reverse of the start plan, which is what makes the phases useful at shutdown:

1. `Serving` stops first, so no new work comes in, and work in flight finishes while what it uses still runs.
2. `Application` stops next, once nothing calls into it.
3. `Initialization` usually has nothing to stop.
4. `Infrastructure` stops next: the pools close once nothing uses them.
5. `Telemetry` stops last, so its exporters flush what the other phases recorded as they stopped.

Within a phase, a service stops before the providers of the milestones it waited for.

## The start plan

Bootable logs the plan before anything starts, each phase with its services, in order, leaving out empty phases, as for an application with a database and a server:

```kotlin
Start plan: Infrastructure[JdbcDataSourceService, ExposedDatabaseService] Initialization[FlywayMigrationService, SchemaVerificationService] Serving[EntryServer]
```

With a shuffled tiebreaker, it names the seed: `Start plan (ties shuffled, seed 42): …​`.

The same computation is a public function, `startPlan(services, startOrder, tiebreaker)`, which returns the services in the order they would start, without starting them.

### Validation

Bootable computes the plan before any lifecycle controller runs, so a plan that can’t be met fails the boot before anything has started. It lists every problem it finds, such as:

- A service in a phase the start order doesn’t have:

  ```kotlin
  SecretsLoader is in phase Secrets, which is not one of the start order's phases: [Telemetry, Infrastructure, Initialization, Application, Serving]. Pass Bootable a StartOrder that includes Secrets.
  ```
- A required milestone that no service provides:

  ```kotlin
  ReportService requires milestone 'db.schema.migrated', but no service provides it. Add a service that provides it, or use 'after' if it is optional.
  ```
- A milestone whose provider is in a later phase:

  ```kotlin
  PriceCalculator (Application) must start after 'pricing.rates.loaded', but its provider ExchangeRates is in Serving, which starts later
  ```
- A cycle, with its path:

  ```kotlin
  Start-order cycle in phase Application: ExchangeRates (after 'pricing.prices.ready') -> PriceCalculator (after 'pricing.rates.loaded') -> ExchangeRates
  ```
- A start order that repeats a phase, or whose default phase isn’t one of its phases.

## Custom start orders

The default phases are in `DefaultStartOrder`, an implementation of `StartOrder`. An application can give `Bootable` its own `StartOrder`. A `StartOrder` has the `phases`, in start order, the `defaultPhase` of a service that names none, and `orderingOf(service)`, which reads a service’s ordering.

To add a phase, delegate to `DefaultStartOrder`, and add yours to its phases. Here, a phase that fetches the secrets, before any connection opens:

```kotlin
enum class AppPhase : Phase { Secrets }

object AppStartOrder : StartOrder by DefaultStartOrder {
  override val phases = listOf(AppPhase.Secrets) + DefaultStartOrder.phases
}

class SecretsLoader : AppService {
  override fun ordering() = Ordering(AppPhase.Secrets)
}
```

Pass it to `Bootable`:

**Vanilla:**

```kotlin
  Bootable(
    setOf(SecretsLoader(), rates, PriceCalculator(rates), OrderConsumer()),
    startOrder = AppStartOrder,
    tiebreaker = serviceOrderConfig(binder).tiebreaker,  // from boot.service.order
  )
```

**Kodein:**

`bootableModule` passes a `StartOrder` binding, if there is one, to `Bootable`:

```kotlin
  import(bootableModule)
  import(hopliteConfigModule)                     // the tiebreaker, from boot.service.order
  bindSingleton<StartOrder> { AppStartOrder }     // passed to Bootable
  bindAppService { singleton { SecretsLoader() } }
```

**Koin:**

`bootableModule()` passes a `StartOrder` definition, if there is one, to `Bootable`:

```kotlin
bootableModule(),
hopliteConfigModule(),                    // the tiebreaker, from boot.service.order
module {
  single<StartOrder> { AppStartOrder }  // passed to Bootable
  single<AppService>(named<SecretsLoader>()) { SecretsLoader() }
},
```

**Metro:**

`BootableDefaultBindings` passes a `StartOrder` binding, if the graph has one, to `Bootable`:

```kotlin
// boot-config-hoplite-metro's ConfigBinder gives Bootable the tiebreaker, from boot.service.order
@ContributesTo(AppScope::class)
interface StartOrderBindings {
  @Provides fun startOrder(): StartOrder = AppStartOrder  // passed to Bootable

  @Provides @IntoSet @SingleIn(AppScope::class)
  fun secretsLoader(): AppService = SecretsLoader()
}
```

**Inara:**

The start order is a parameter of `bootableModule(…​)`:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface OrderedAppModule : ConfigModule, BootableModule {
  @AppServices val secretsLoader: SecretsLoader
}

fun orderedAppModule() = OrderedAppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),                         // the tiebreaker, from boot.service.order
  bootableModule = bootableModule(startOrder = AppStartOrder),  // a parameter, passed to Bootable
  secretsLoader = Binding.single { SecretsLoader() },
)
```

Bootable’s own services keep the `DefaultPhase`s they declare, so the list mixes the two. A start order can also replace the phases with its own, mapping each `DefaultPhase` onto one of them in `orderingOf`, or use `orderingOf` to place a service it didn’t write. A phase that a service is in, and the start order lacks, fails the boot, so nothing is silently misplaced.

The [Custom start order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/start-order.html.md) example adds a phase at the other end, after `Serving`, for a service that announces the application is ready once its server listens.

## Reference

- [`Ordering`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-ordering/index.html): a service’s place in the order
- [`DefaultPhase`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-default-phase/index.html): the default phases
- [`Milestone`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-milestone/index.html) and [`milestone`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/milestone.html): milestones
- [`StartOrder`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-start-order/index.html) and [`DefaultStartOrder`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-default-start-order/index.html): the start order
- [`Tiebreaker`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-start-order/-tiebreaker/index.html): how ties are broken
- [`ServiceOrderConfig`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/-service-order-config/index.html): the `boot.service.order` config
- [`startPlan`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.boot/start-plan.html): the start plan, for tests
- [`DbMilestones`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-db-jdbc/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.db.jdbc/-db-milestones/index.html) and [`HttpClientMilestones`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-client-http-ktor/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.client.http.ktor/-http-client-milestones/index.html): Bootable’s milestones

# Configuration

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html

> Typed config classes, bound from HOCON and the environment by Hoplite, with secrets masked.

An application’s config is a set of typed classes, each bound from a section of the config by a `ConfigBinder`. `boot-config-common` defines the `ConfigBinder`, which Bootable’s own modules read their config with, and `boot-config-hoplite` implements it with [Hoplite](https://github.com/sksamuel/hoplite), from HOCON files, system properties, and the environment.

Config isn’t a service, so it has no lifecycle phase of its own. It is bound while the application is built, in the `boot { }` block, which runs after logging is initialized, so a config error is logged, and fails the start before any service starts.

## Modules

An application adds the config library, `boot-config-hoplite`. `boot-config-common` comes with it, and with every module that reads config.

| Module | What it provides |
| --- | --- |
| **Config library: choose one** |  |
| `boot-config-hoplite` | `ConfigBinder` over Hoplite, from HOCON and the environment |
| **Common: comes with the config library, and the modules that read config** |  |
| `boot-config-common` | `ConfigBinder`, and `Masked`, for secrets in config |

## Install

**Vanilla:**

```kotlin
dependencies {
  implementation("com.github.rocketraman.bootable:boot-config-hoplite:3.1.0-SNAPSHOT")
}
```

**Kodein:**

```kotlin
dependencies {
  implementation("com.github.rocketraman.bootable:boot-config-hoplite-kodein:3.1.0-SNAPSHOT")
}
```

**Koin:**

```kotlin
dependencies {
  implementation("com.github.rocketraman.bootable:boot-config-hoplite-koin:3.1.0-SNAPSHOT")
}
```

**Metro:**

```kotlin
plugins {
  id("dev.zacsweers.metro") version "1.4.5"
}

dependencies {
  implementation("com.github.rocketraman.bootable:boot-config-hoplite-metro:3.1.0-SNAPSHOT")
}
```

**Inara:**

```kotlin
plugins {
  id("com.google.devtools.ksp") version "2.3.13"
}

dependencies {
  implementation("com.github.rocketraman.bootable:boot-config-hoplite-inara:3.1.0-SNAPSHOT")
  ksp("org.kodein.di.inara:inara-processor:0.3.0")
}
```

## Configure

Hoplite reads these sources, each overriding the ones below it:

1. Environment variables, such as `GREETING_MESSAGE` for `greeting.message`; see [Environment variables](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md#environment-variables).
2. System properties with the `config.override.` prefix, such as `-Dconfig.override.greeting.message=hi`.
3. `~/.userconfig.conf`, in the user’s home directory, and `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/hoplite.conf`, if they exist.
4. `application-local.conf`, on the classpath, if it exists: for settings on a developer’s machine, kept out of version control.
5. `application.conf`, on the classpath, which must exist.

Each config class reads one section, named by its path:

```hocon
greeting {
  message = "hello from Bootable"
  apiKey = ${?GREETING_API_KEY}  (1)
}

server {
  host-port = ":8080"  (2)
}
```

- (1) From the environment variable, if it is set; see [Substitutions](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md#substitutions).
- (2) A key matches its property in any case, and with or without dashes, so `host-port`, as here, and `hostPort`, as the property is spelled, are the same key.

### Config classes

A config class is a data class, with a property for each key in its section. A property with a default, or a nullable one, is optional; any other fails the bind when its key is missing.

```kotlin
data class GreetingConfig(
  val message: String,
  val apiKey: Secret,                  // masked in the config report
  val retries: Int = 3,                // optional, with its default
)

data class ServerConfig(
  override val hostPort: String,       // ":8080", "localhost:8080", or "localhost"
) : HostPort
```

`HostPort`, from `boot-config-common`, is a `hostPort` string, such as `localhost:8080` or `:8080`, with helpers to read it: `host()`, which defaults to `0.0.0.0`, `port(default)`, `portOrNull()`, and `inetAddress()`. The Ktor server takes its address as a `HostPort`.

Hoplite decodes the usual types: strings, numbers, booleans, durations such as `5s`, lists, sets, maps, and nested data classes. An enum value matches its entry’s name in any case, so `fail`, `Fail`, and `FAIL` are all `Fail`. A sealed type is chosen by its subtype’s name, in a `_type` key next to the subtype’s properties, such as `tiebreaker { _type = Shuffled, seed = 42 }`.

### Secrets

The config classes of Bootable’s own modules declare a secret, such as a password, an API key, or an auth header, as `Masked`, from `boot-config-common`. Their config classes depend only on `boot-config-common`, not on a config library, so they can’t use the library’s own type for secrets. A `Masked`'s `toString` is `****`, so a config class that holds one prints safely; read the secret with `value`. `boot-config-hoplite` decodes a `Masked` from a string or a number.

In your own config classes, declare a secret with Hoplite’s `Secret`, as `GreetingConfig.apiKey` does above. Bootable doesn’t aim to make config libraries interchangeable, so `Masked` is for its own modules.

### The config report

When it binds a section, `boot-config-hoplite` prints a report of the section’s keys, each with its value and where it came from, and the keys in it that its config class doesn’t read. It prints to standard output, which Bootable [logs](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md#standard-streams), once logging is initialized. The report masks these values:

- a `Masked` value, wherever it is: in a data class, a map, or a list;
- a Hoplite `Secret`;
- a value whose name contains `secret`, `credential`, or `pass`;
- a value its source marks as a secret.

The report shows values as they were loaded, before Hoplite’s resolvers run, so it shows `${{ env:DB_PASSWORD }}`, not the password. Turn it off with `report = false`; see [Customize the binder](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md#customize).

### Environment variables

An environment variable overrides the key whose path it spells, in upper case, with `_` in place of each `.`: `GREETING_MESSAGE` sets `greeting.message`. A camel case key is spelled without a separator: `DB_POOL_MAXIMUMPOOLSIZE` sets `db.pool.maximumPoolSize`.

An environment variable overrides a map entry, or a property of one, keeping the entry’s key as config spells it. With `http.client.named.myClient { baseUrl = "http://localhost:8001/" }` in config, `HTTP_CLIENT_NAMED_MYCLIENT_BASEURL=http://localhost:8002/` changes the `baseUrl` of the `myClient` client, rather than adding a client named `MYCLIENT`. An entry that only the environment defines is keyed as the environment variable spells it, in upper case.

### Substitutions

A value can name an environment variable, or another value, in two ways.

HOCON’s own substitutions work anywhere, in maps and lists too, and are resolved when HOCON parses the file:

```hocon
db.jdbc.dataSourceProperties {
  sslmode = ${?DB_SSLMODE}  (1)
}
greeting.message = ${app.name}  (2)
```

- (1) The environment variable, if it is set; without it, the key is left unset, so a property with a default keeps it. `${DB_SSLMODE}`, without the `?`, fails the parse when the variable isn’t set.
- (2) Another value in the config.

Hoplite’s resolvers name an environment variable, a system property, or another value, with a fallback if you like:

```hocon
db.jdbc {
  host = "${{ env:DB_HOST }}"
  port = "${{ env:DB_PORT:-5432 }}"  (1)
  username = "${{ sysprop:db.user }}"
  database = "${{ ref:app.name }}"
}
```

- (1) The fallback, after `:-`, when the variable isn’t set.

A resolver that resolves to nothing, and has no fallback, fails the bind, even for a property with a default. A resolver works only in a property whose value is a single string, which can then be decoded as another type, such as the `Int` port above. In the entries of a map, a list, or a set, it is left as literal text: use HOCON’s `${?VAR}` there.

Hoplite’s older preprocessor syntax, `${VAR}` in a quoted string, or `{{key}}`, is not expanded, and is left as literal text.

### Bootable’s own config

Each Bootable module reads its own section, such as `db` for the database, `http.client` for the HTTP clients, `telemetry` for OpenTelemetry, or `env` for the environment. A module’s page shows its section; [the database’s](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/index.html.md#_configure), for example. With a DI, a module’s bindings bind its config from the graph’s `ConfigBinder`; wired by hand, you bind it, and pass it to the module’s constructor.

Bootable itself reads two optional sections, if there is a `ConfigBinder`: `boot.service.order`, how services the start order leaves tied are started, and `health.readiness`, the readiness checks' settings.

## Wire

**Vanilla:**

Build the binder with `hopliteConfigBinder()`, and bind each section with `config<T>(path)`:

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  val binder = hopliteConfigBinder()
  Bootable(
    setOf(GreetingService(binder.config<GreetingConfig>("greeting"))),
  )
}
```

**Kodein:**

Import `hopliteConfigModule`, which binds the `ConfigBinder`, and bind each section with `bindConfig<T>(path)`, which decodes it once:

```kotlin
fun appDI() = DI {
  import(bootableModule)
  import(hopliteConfigModule)  // binds the ConfigBinder
  bindConfig<GreetingConfig>("greeting")
  bindAppService { singleton { new(::GreetingService) } }
}

fun main() = boot {
  appDI().direct.instance<Bootable>()
}
```

**Koin:**

Include `hopliteConfigModule()`, which defines the `ConfigBinder`, and define each section with `config<T>(path)`, a `single` that decodes it once:

```kotlin
fun appKoin() = koinApplication {
  modules(
    bootableModule(),
    hopliteConfigModule(),  // defines the ConfigBinder
    module {
      config<GreetingConfig>("greeting")
      single<AppService>(named<GreetingService>()) { GreetingService(get()) }
    },
  )
}.koin

fun main() = boot {
  appKoin().get<Bootable>()
}
```

**Metro:**

`boot-config-hoplite-metro` contributes the `ConfigBinder` on its own. Bind each section in a contributed interface that extends `ConfigBinderProvider`, which gives it the binder, so each binding is a type and a path:

```kotlin
// boot-config-hoplite-metro contributes the ConfigBinder; each config binding is a type and a key
@ContributesTo(ConfigurationScope::class)
interface GreetingConfigBindings : ConfigBinderProvider {
  @Provides fun greetingConfig(): GreetingConfig = config("greeting")
}

@DependencyGraph(ConfigurationScope::class, additionalScopes = [BootScope::class])
interface ConfigurationGraph : BootableGraph

fun main() = boot {
  createGraph<ConfigurationGraph>().bootable
}
```

A graph without a `ConfigBinder` fails to compile with a missing binding.

**Inara:**

Compose `hopliteConfigModule()`, the `ConfigModule` every other module reads, and bind each section with `config(…​)`:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface AppModule : ConfigModule, BootableModule {
  val greetingConfig: GreetingConfig
  @AppServices val greetingService: GreetingService
}

fun appModule() = AppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),  // provides the ConfigBinder
  bootableModule = bootableModule(),
  greetingConfig = config("greeting"),   // decoded once, from the ConfigBinder
  greetingService = Binding.single { GreetingService(greetingConfig) },
)

fun main() = boot {
  appModule().bootable
}
```

## Customize the binder

`hopliteConfigBinder` takes optional parameters:

- `withConfigStage1`, `withConfigStage2`, `withConfigStage3`: hooks on Hoplite’s `ConfigLoaderBuilder`, to add sources, resolvers, or anything else. Sources added in stage 1 override the environment variables; in stage 2, they are between the user settings and `application-local.conf`; in stage 3, below `application.conf`. Hoplite’s modules for secret stores, such as Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, and Azure Key Vault, add their resolvers this way, with `addResolver`.
- `decoders`: Hoplite decoders for your own types, which can also be registered with Java’s `ServiceLoader`.
- `report`: whether to print [the config report](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md#report); `true` by default.
- `secretsPolicy` and `obfuscator`: which values the report masks, and how; Hoplite’s `StandardSecretsPolicy` and `StrictObfuscator` by default. A `Masked` value is masked whatever the policy.
- `strict`: fail a bind when its section has a key the config class has no property for; `false` by default.
- `environmentVariables`: the environment variables, for the environment variable source and `${{ env:VAR }}`; `System.getenv()` by default. HOCON’s own `${?VAR}` substitutions read the process environment, not these.

**Vanilla:**

```kotlin
fun customBinder(): ConfigBinder = hopliteConfigBinder(
  // above application.conf, below everything else
  withConfigStage2 = { addPropertySource(PropertySource.file(java.io.File("/etc/greeter/greeter.conf"), optional = true)) },
  report = false,  // no config report at start
  strict = true,   // fail on a key in a section that its config class has no property for
)
```

**Kodein:**

Bind your own `ConfigBinder`, in place of `hopliteConfigModule`:

```kotlin
fun customDI() = DI {
  import(bootableModule)
  // in place of hopliteConfigModule
  bindSingleton<ConfigBinder> { hopliteConfigBinder(report = false, strict = true) }
}
```

**Koin:**

Define your own `ConfigBinder`, in place of `hopliteConfigModule()`:

```kotlin
fun customKoin() = koinApplication {
  modules(
    bootableModule(),
    // in place of hopliteConfigModule()
    module { single<ConfigBinder> { hopliteConfigBinder(report = false, strict = true) } },
  )
}.koin
```

**Metro:**

Provide your own `ConfigBinder`, and name Bootable’s binding containers in the graph, rather than discovering them, so `HopliteConfigBindings`'s default isn’t in the graph too:

```kotlin
@BindingContainer
object CustomConfigBinder {
  @Provides @SingleIn(BootScope::class)
  fun configBinder(): ConfigBinder = hopliteConfigBinder(report = false, strict = true)
}

// Bootable's bindings named, not discovered, so HopliteConfigBindings' default ConfigBinder isn't in the graph
@DependencyGraph(ConfigurationScope::class, bindingContainers = [BootableDefaultBindings::class, CustomConfigBinder::class])
interface CustomConfigGraph : BootableGraph
```

A container named this way isn’t discovered, so name every one the graph needs, such as `EnvironmentBindings` for [the environment](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/environment/index.html.md).

**Inara:**

Build your own `ConfigModule`, and pass it in place of `hopliteConfigModule()`:

```kotlin
// passed as the configModule, in place of hopliteConfigModule()
val customConfigModule = ConfigModule(
  configBinder = Binding.single { hopliteConfigBinder(report = false, strict = true) },
)
```

## Example

`examples/wiring-vanilla`, `examples/wiring-kodein`, `examples/wiring-koin`, and `examples/wiring-metro` each bind a `greeting` section from `application.conf`, and log it when the application starts. From the repository root, run yours:

**Vanilla:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-vanilla:run
```

**Kodein:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-kodein:run
```

**Koin:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-koin:run
```

**Metro:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-metro:run
```

**Inara:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-inara:run
```

It logs `greeting: hello from Bootable`; try it with `GREETING_MESSAGE=hi` set.

## Reference

- [`ConfigBinder`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-config-common/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.config/-config-binder/index.html): binds a config section to a type
- [`config`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-config-common/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.config/config.html): `config<T>(path)`
- `bindConfig<T>(path)`, in `boot-config-common-kodein`: binds a section in a Kodein module; `bindConfigAs<T, C>(path)` binds a section decoded as a `C` as its supertype `T`
- `config<T>(path)`, in `boot-config-common-koin`'s `com.github.rocketraman.bootable.config.koin` package: defines a section in a Koin module; `configAs<T, C>(path)` defines a section decoded as a `C` as its supertype `T`
- [`Masked`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-config-common/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.config/-masked/index.html): a secret in Bootable’s own config classes
- [`HostPort`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-config-common/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.config.common/-host-port/index.html): a host and port
- [`hopliteConfigBinder`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-config-hoplite/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.config/hoplite-config-binder.html): the Hoplite binder, and its parameters
- [Hoplite](https://github.com/sksamuel/hoplite)'s own documentation
