# Periodic work

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html

> PeriodicAppService: a loop in the background, gated on the leader or the application's health, with a trace for each run.

`boot-periodic` provides `PeriodicAppService`, the loop that an application would otherwise write by hand: every few seconds or minutes, send the notifications that are pending, or sweep what has expired. The application writes only the work.

It is in the `Serving` phase by default, as something that brings work into the application, so it starts after the services its work uses, and stops before them.

## The work

A loop has a name, its config, an optional gate, and its work, a suspending function:

```kotlin
  PeriodicAppService(
    "notifications",                      // its name, in its log messages and its trace
    binder.config("notifications.loop"),  // its PeriodicConfig
    PeriodicGate.leader(leaderElection),  // on the leader only
  ) {
    notifications.sendPending()
  }
```

It runs the work on a coroutine in the service’s scope, on `Dispatchers.Default` unless its `dispatcher` says otherwise. Each run starts a fixed delay, the `interval`, after the previous run ends, so runs never overlap, and a run that takes longer than the interval delays the next rather than piling up behind it.

Work that blocks, such as JDBC calls, should switch to `Dispatchers.IO` for the calls that block, or run the loop there:

```kotlin
  PeriodicAppService("purge", binder.config("purge.loop"), dispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) {
    purge()  // JDBC calls, which block
  }
```

The service notes when each run started, and when one last succeeded and failed, in `lastStarted`, `lastSucceeded`, and `lastFailed`, by its `kotlin.time.Clock`, with `consecutiveFailures` and `isRunning`, such as for a health check that the loop isn’t stuck.

## Configure

Each loop has a config section of the application’s choosing, decoded as a `PeriodicConfig`. Every setting has a default, so the section is optional:

```hocon
notifications.loop {
  interval = 5s                (1)
  runTimeout = 1m              (2)
  maxConsecutiveFailures = 10  (3)
  onFailureLimit = Shutdown    (4)
}
```

- (1) Sets how often the loop runs: the delay between one run’s end and the next one’s start, so runs never overlap; a minute by default.
- (2) Cancels a run that hangs, such as on a call that never returns, and counts it as a failure; no limit by default.
- (3) Gives up on a loop that keeps failing, such as on a record that fails every run, rather than failing forever; no limit by default.
- (4) Stops the application, with exit code 1, once it gives up, by failing the service’s scope, so that its platform restarts it, or an operator notices. The default, `StopLoop`, stops the loop and logs an error, while the rest of the application runs on.

The others are `enabled`, `initialDelay`, before the first run, and `shutdownTimeout`, how long shutdown waits for a run in progress before cancelling it, 10 seconds: see [all the settings](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-config/index.html).

## Gates

Before each run, the loop asks its `PeriodicGate`, and skips the run when the gate is closed; it asks again an interval later.

- `PeriodicGate.Always`, the default, is always open: every instance runs the loop.
- `PeriodicGate.leader(leaderElection)` is open while this instance is the [leader](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md), so only one instance runs the loop; for a leader that pauses, a run that writes sends its [fencing token](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#fencing) with each write.
- `PeriodicGate.running(health)` is open while the application is running: once every service has started, and until shutdown begins. A loop in the `Serving` phase starts with the last services to start, so this holds its runs back only until the others in that phase, such as the HTTP server, have started too.
- `and` combines two gates: open when both are.

```kotlin
  PeriodicAppService(
    "notifications",
    binder.config("notifications.loop"),
    PeriodicGate.leader(leaderElection) and PeriodicGate.running(health),
  ) {
    notifications.sendPending()
  }
```

A gate that closes while a run is in progress, as the leader gate does when this instance stops leading, cancels the run, which isn’t counted as a failure. Cancellation is cooperative: work that blocks, such as a JDBC call, stops only at its next suspension point, unless it blocks in `runInterruptible`.

A gate of your own is a `fun interface`: `isOpen()` must return promptly, without blocking. A gate that can close during a run says so by overriding `awaitClosed()`, which suspends until it closes.

## Failures

A run that throws is handed to the loop’s `PeriodicFailureHandler`, and the loop carries on, unless `maxConsecutiveFailures` runs in a row have failed. The default handler, `PeriodicFailureHandler.Log`, logs the failure as an error. A handler of your own runs on the loop’s coroutine, so it must return promptly; what it throws is logged.

```kotlin
  PeriodicAppService(
    "notifications",
    binder.config("notifications.loop"),
    onFailure = PeriodicFailureHandler { service, failure, consecutiveFailures ->
      // in place of the default, which logs each failure as an error
      if (consecutiveFailures < 3) log.warn(failure) { "$service failed" }
      else log.error(failure) { "$service failed $consecutiveFailures times in a row" }
    },
  ) {
    notifications.sendPending()
  }
```

A run the gate skips neither fails nor succeeds, and a run that `runTimeout` cancels fails. `maxConsecutiveFailures` guards against a poison pill, such as a record that fails every run, which would otherwise fail forever.

## Start and shutdown

The loop’s first run is `initialDelay` after it starts. On shutdown, it starts no further run, and doesn’t wait for the interval: it waits up to `shutdownTimeout` for a run in progress to finish, and then cancels it.

To run a loop in another phase, or after a milestone, pass its `ordering`.

## Wire

`PeriodicServices` holds what the application’s loops share, their default gate, clock, interceptors, and failure handler, so each loop needs only its name, config, and work: `periodic.create(name, config) { …​ }`.

**Vanilla:**

Build a `PeriodicServices`, or construct each `PeriodicAppService` yourself, and pass the loops to `Bootable` with the other services:

```kotlin
  val health = HealthLifecycleController()
  // what the application's loops share: here, their gate, so they run only once the application is running
  val periodic = PeriodicServices(gate = PeriodicGate.running(health))

  return Bootable(
    setOf(
      periodic.create("notifications", binder.config("notifications.loop")) { notifications.sendPending() },
      // ... and the services the loops use
    ),
    defaultLifecycleControllers().withHealthLifecycleController(health),
  )
```

**Kodein:**

Import `periodicModule`, which binds `PeriodicServices`, and add each loop to the app-service set:

```kotlin
fun periodicDI() = DI {
  import(bootableModule)
  import(hopliteConfigModule)
  import(periodicModule)  // PeriodicServices, gated on the LeaderElection binding, if there is one

  bindSingleton { new(::Notifications) }
  // each loop has a PeriodicConfig of its own, so tag it
  bindConfig<PeriodicConfig>("notifications.loop", tag = "notifications")
  bindAppService {
    singleton {
      instance<PeriodicServices>().create("notifications", instance("notifications")) {
        instance<Notifications>().sendPending()
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Its gate is `PeriodicGate.leader` of the `LeaderElection` binding, if there is one, such as `kubernetesLeaderElectionModule`'s; otherwise every instance runs the loops. Its clock is the `kotlin.time.Clock` binding, if there is one, and its interceptors are those of the `Set<PeriodicRunInterceptor>` it opens.

**Koin:**

Include `periodicModule()`, which defines `PeriodicServices`, and add each loop to the app services, with a qualifier of its own:

```kotlin
fun periodicKoin() = koinApplication {
  modules(
    bootableModule(),
    hopliteConfigModule(),
    periodicModule(),  // PeriodicServices, gated on the LeaderElection definition, if there is one
    module {
      single { Notifications() }
      // each loop has a PeriodicConfig of its own, so qualify it
      config<PeriodicConfig>("notifications.loop", named("notifications"))
      single<AppService>(named("notifications")) {
        val notifications = get<Notifications>()
        get<PeriodicServices>().create("notifications", get(named("notifications"))) {
          notifications.sendPending()
        }
      }
    },
  )
}.koin
```

Its gate is `PeriodicGate.leader` of the `LeaderElection` definition, if there is one, such as `kubernetesLeaderElectionModule()`'s; otherwise every instance runs the loops. Its clock is the `kotlin.time.Clock` definition, if there is one, and its interceptors are every `PeriodicRunInterceptor` definition.

**Metro:**

`boot-periodic-metro` contributes `PeriodicServices`; contribute each loop to the app-service set:

```kotlin
@ContributesTo(BackgroundScope::class)
interface NotificationBindings {
  @Provides @SingleIn(BackgroundScope::class)
  fun notifications(): Notifications = Notifications()

  // PeriodicServices is gated on the graph's LeaderElection, if it has one
  @Provides @IntoSet
  fun notificationsLoop(periodic: PeriodicServices, binder: ConfigBinder, notifications: Notifications): AppService =
    periodic.create("notifications", binder.config("notifications.loop")) { notifications.sendPending() }
}
```

Its gate is `PeriodicGate.leader` of the graph’s `LeaderElection`, if it has one, such as `boot-leader-k8s-metro`'s; otherwise every instance runs the loops. Its clock is the graph’s `kotlin.time.Clock`, if it has one, and its interceptors are the contributed `PeriodicRunInterceptor` set.

**Inara:**

Compose `periodicModule()`, which provides `PeriodicServices`, and mark each loop `@AppServices`:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface PeriodicAppModule :
  ConfigModule, BootableModule, LeaderElectionModule, OpenTelemetryApiModule, PeriodicModule {
  val notifications: Notifications
  @AppServices val notificationsLoop: PeriodicAppService
}

fun periodicAppModule() = PeriodicAppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),
  bootableModule = bootableModule(),
  leaderElectionModule = AlwaysLeaderModule,         // required: every instance runs the loops
  openTelemetryApiModule = NoopOpenTelemetryModule,  // required: no tracing of the runs
  periodicModule = periodicModule(),                 // periodicServices, gated on the leaderElection
  notifications = Binding.single { Notifications() },
  notificationsLoop = Binding.single {
    periodicServices.create("notifications", configBinder.config("notifications.loop")) { notifications.sendPending() }
  },
)
```

A loop that needs another gate passes it to `create`, in place of the shared one.

## Telemetry

`boot-periodic` can make each run a trace of its own, with `periodicTracing`, a `PeriodicRunInterceptor`: a root span named for the loop, such as `periodic notifications`, so that the run’s queries and log events belong to it. The span carries the loop’s name as `bootable.periodic.service`, and a run that fails ends it with an error status and the exception recorded. A run the gate skips isn’t traced.

It depends only on the OpenTelemetry API, through [`boot-telemetry-otel-common`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md#spans); the application’s SDK, such as [`boot-telemetry-otel`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md)'s, records the traces.

**Vanilla:**

Give `periodicTracing` to `PeriodicServices`, or to each `PeriodicAppService`, as an interceptor:

```kotlin
  PeriodicServices(
    PeriodicGate.leader(leaderElection),
    interceptors = listOf(periodicTracing(telemetry.openTelemetry)),  // a trace for each run
  )
```

**Kodein:**

`periodicModule` traces each run whenever there is an `OpenTelemetry` binding, such as `openTelemetryModule`'s, and not at all when there is none:

```kotlin
  import(openTelemetryModule)  // the application's OpenTelemetry, from boot-telemetry-otel: periodicModule traces each run
```

The tracing is the outermost interceptor, around those of the `Set<PeriodicRunInterceptor>`.

**Koin:**

`periodicModule()` traces each run whenever there is an `OpenTelemetry` definition, such as `openTelemetryModule()`'s, and not at all when there is none:

```kotlin
includes(openTelemetryModule())  // the application's OpenTelemetry, from boot-telemetry-otel: periodicModule() traces each run
```

The tracing is the outermost interceptor, around those of the `PeriodicRunInterceptor` definitions.

**Metro:**

`boot-periodic-metro` traces each run whenever the graph has an `OpenTelemetry`, such as `boot-telemetry-otel-metro`'s, and not at all when it has none: there is nothing to wire. The tracing is the outermost interceptor, around the contributed ones.

**Inara:**

`periodicModule()` requires an `OpenTelemetryApiModule`, and traces each run through it: compose `openTelemetryModule()` to trace, or `NoopOpenTelemetryModule` for none:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface TracedPeriodicAppModule :
  // OpenTelemetryModule in place of OpenTelemetryApiModule: it is one, with the SDK
  ConfigModule, BootableModule, LeaderElectionModule, OpenTelemetryModule, PeriodicModule

fun tracedPeriodicAppModule() = TracedPeriodicAppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),
  bootableModule = bootableModule(),
  leaderElectionModule = AlwaysLeaderModule,
  // the application's OpenTelemetry, from boot-telemetry-otel: periodicModule traces each run
  openTelemetryModule = openTelemetryModule(),
  periodicModule = periodicModule(),
)
```

### Sampling, or no tracing

Each run’s trace is sampled as the SDK’s sampler decides, such as at the configured `sampleRatio`. For a loop that runs rarely enough that every run’s trace is worth keeping, sample them all with `Sample.Always`. With Kodein or Metro, a `PeriodicTracingOptions` binding sets that, with Koin, a `PeriodicTracingOptions` definition, and with Inara, `periodicModule`'s `tracingOptions`; with `enabled = false`, it turns the tracing off:

**Vanilla:**

```kotlin
  PeriodicServices(interceptors = listOf(periodicTracing(telemetry.openTelemetry, Sample.Always)))
```

**Kodein:**

```kotlin
  bindSingleton { PeriodicTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always) }  // or enabled = false, to trace no run
```

**Koin:**

```kotlin
single { PeriodicTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always) }  // or enabled = false, to trace no run
```

**Metro:**

Provide it in a binding container that the graph names:

```kotlin
@BindingContainer
object AlwaysSampledPeriodicTracing {
  @Provides fun periodicTracingOptions(): PeriodicTracingOptions =
    PeriodicTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always)  // or enabled = false
}

@DependencyGraph(
  BackgroundScope::class,
  additionalScopes = [BootScope::class],
  bindingContainers = [AlwaysSampledPeriodicTracing::class],
)
interface AlwaysSampledPeriodicGraph : BootableGraph
```

**Inara:**

The options are a parameter of the builder:

```kotlin
  // a parameter of the builder; or enabled = false, to trace no run
  periodicModule = periodicModule(tracingOptions = PeriodicTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always)),
```

The setting applies to every loop that shares the interceptor: with Kodein, Koin, Metro, or Inara, every loop created from `PeriodicServices`.

## Reference

- [`PeriodicAppService`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-app-service/index.html): the loop
- [`PeriodicConfig`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-config/index.html): its settings
- [`PeriodicGate`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-gate/index.html): whether it runs this time round
- [`PeriodicFailureHandler`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-failure-handler/index.html): what it does with a run that failed
- [`PeriodicServices`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-services/index.html): what the loops share
- [`PeriodicRunInterceptor`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-run-interceptor/index.html): code around each run
- [`periodicTracing`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/periodic-tracing.html): a trace for each run
- [`PeriodicTracingOptions`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-periodic/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.periodic/-periodic-tracing-options/index.html): how the DI flavours trace the runs

# Leader election

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html

> LeaderElection: whether this instance leads, by a Kubernetes Lease, or always, and a fencing token for its writes.

`boot-leader-common` defines `LeaderElection`: whether this instance is the leader of the application’s instances, such as the replicas of a Kubernetes deployment. At most one of them leads at any time, as long as the leader doesn’t pause for too long; its [fencing token](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#fencing) covers a leader that does, where the work writes. Use it for work that only one instance should do, such as a [periodic loop](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html.md#gates) that sends pending notifications.

`boot-leader-k8s` elects the leader among an application’s pods with a Kubernetes Lease. It is in the `Infrastructure` phase, so it leads, if it can, before the loops that ask it start, and stops after them.

Work that db-scheduler runs needs no leader: it runs each execution on one instance by locking its row; see [Scheduled tasks (db-scheduler)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/scheduler.html.md). For when leadership and fencing are the right tool, and what to use when they aren’t, see [When to lead, and when not to](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#right-tool).

## LeaderElection

`leadership` is a `StateFlow<Boolean>`, which is true while this instance leads. `isLeader()` asks whether it leads now, and `awaitLeadership()` suspends until it does:

```kotlin
class Housekeeping(private val leaderElection: LeaderElection) {
  private val log = logger()

  /** Asks whether this instance leads now. */
  fun cleanUpIfLeader() {
    if (leaderElection.isLeader()) cleanUp()
  }

  /** Suspends until this instance leads. */
  suspend fun cleanUpOnceLeading() {
    leaderElection.awaitLeadership()
    cleanUp()
  }

  /** Follows each change of leadership, as it happens. */
  suspend fun logLeadership() {
    leaderElection.leadership.collect { leading -> log.info { if (leading) "Leading" else "Not leading" } }
  }

  private fun cleanUp() {
    // ...
  }
}
```

`fencingToken` is the current lease term’s fencing token, or null while this instance doesn’t lead; see [Fencing tokens](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#fencing).

The [leader gate](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html.md#gates), `PeriodicGate.leader(leaderElection)`, asks it before each run, and cancels a run in progress when `leadership` turns false.

There are two implementations:

- `AlwaysLeader`, in `boot-leader-common`, always leads: for an application that runs as one instance, and for running locally. Its `fencingToken` is always 0.
- `KubernetesLeaderElection`, in `boot-leader-k8s`, holds a Lease.

## Kubernetes

`KubernetesLeaderElection` elects a leader as Kubernetes’s own controllers elect theirs, following client-go’s leader election: the leader is the pod that holds a `coordination.k8s.io/v1` Lease.

- The leader renews the Lease every `retryPeriod`, and gives up leadership when it hasn’t renewed it within `renewDeadline`.
- The other pods try to take the Lease every `retryPeriod`, and take it once it hasn’t been renewed for `leaseDuration`.
- On shutdown, the leader releases the Lease, so another pod takes over at once, rather than after `leaseDuration`.

Starting it makes the first attempt to take the Lease, and fails the start if the API server refuses it access, with a 401 or 403 status, such as when the pod’s service account lacks the permission, since retrying wouldn’t fix that. It then keeps trying, or renewing, in the background, and retries whatever fails.

### Configure

It reads `leader.kubernetes`, where only the Lease’s name is required:

```hocon
leader.kubernetes {
  leaseName = notifications-leader  (1)
  leaseDuration = 30s               (2)
  renewDeadline = 20s               (3)
}
```

- (1) Names the Lease the instances compete for: one for each application, which every instance of it names alike, and no other application does.
- (2) Tolerates longer pauses of the leader, such as for garbage collection, at the cost of a slower takeover when a leader dies without releasing the Lease; by default, 15 seconds.
- (3) Keeps the margin between the two, 10 seconds here, 5 by default, which is how long the leader’s work has to stop, and the longest pause the guarantee survives; see [Timing](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#timing). `leaseDuration` must be longer than `renewDeadline`, and `renewDeadline` longer than `retryPeriod`, 2 seconds by default, or decoding the config fails.

To run outside Kubernetes, such as locally, with the same wiring, set `assumeLeader = true` in that environment’s config: the instance skips the election, and always leads, with a fencing token of 0.

The API server’s address comes from `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` and `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT`, which Kubernetes gives every pod, unless `apiServer` is set. The service account’s token, and its namespace, are read from `serviceAccountDir`, `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount` by default. The others include `namespace` and `identity`, by default the pod’s own namespace and name, `retryPeriod`, `requestTimeout`, `releaseOnShutdown`, and `httpClient` (see [The API server’s client](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#the-api-server)): see [all the settings](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-leader-k8s/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.leader.k8s/-kubernetes-leader-election-config/index.html).

### Permissions

The pod’s service account needs a Role that allows `get`, `create`, and `update` on `leases` in the `coordination.k8s.io` API group, in the Lease’s namespace, bound to it:

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: leader-election
rules:
  - apiGroups: [coordination.k8s.io]
    resources: [leases]
    verbs: [get, create, update]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: leader-election
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: leader-election
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: notifications  # the pod's service account
```

Each request authenticates with the service account’s token, read from its file for each request, since Kubernetes rotates it.

### The API server’s client

It talks to the API server’s REST API through one of the application’s own [Ktor clients](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/client.html.md), from `boot-client-http-ktor`, rather than through a Kubernetes client library: leader election needs only three calls on one Lease. So the API server’s TLS, timeouts, and retries are configured as every other HTTP call the application makes is, and the engine is the application’s choice.

It uses the client named by `httpClient`, `kubernetes` by default, or the default client if there is none of that name. In a cluster, that client trusts the API server with no TLS config of the application’s: `kubernetesClientDefaults` defaults its trust store to the service account’s CA certificate, `ca.crt`, so `leaseName` is the only setting the election needs. The application’s own config of the client, in `http.client.named.kubernetes`, applies over that default, and its `tls`, if it sets one, replaces it, such as to trust another CA:

```hocon
http.client.named.kubernetes {
  tls.trustStore { path = "/etc/k8s/ca.crt", type = PEM }  (1)
}
```

- (1) Trusts another CA’s certificates in place of the service account’s `ca.crt`, such as for an API server outside the cluster.

The Kodein, Koin, Metro, and Inara flavours contribute the default; with vanilla wiring, pass `kubernetesClientDefaults(config)` to `KtorClientService`, as [Wire](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#wire) shows.

The election is in the same phase as the clients, after their `HttpClientMilestones.ClientsReady` milestone, so it stops, releasing the Lease, before they close.

### Timing

Two pods never lead at once, because a leader steps down before another pod can take over:

- The leader steps down `renewDeadline` after it sent its last successful renewal, even if a request is still in flight then.
- Another pod takes the Lease only `leaseDuration` after it saw that renewal, which was after it was sent.
- Both are timed by each pod’s monotonic clock, so the pods' clocks need not agree, and a clock that jumps elects no second leader; the Lease’s own times are only informational.

The leader’s work must stop within the margin between the two, 5 seconds by default, once `leadership` turns false: the leader gate cancels a run in progress then. The guarantee holds as long as the leader doesn’t pause, such as for a long garbage collection or a suspended VM, for longer than that margin, since a paused pod can’t step down: it would then carry on as though it still led. A [fencing token](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md#fencing) covers that pause, where the work writes.

A leader that stops without releasing the Lease, such as one that crashes, is replaced within about `leaseDuration`. `renewDeadline` must be longer than `retryPeriod`, and `leaseDuration` longer than `renewDeadline`.

## Fencing tokens

A leader that pauses, such as for a long garbage collection or a suspended VM, can’t step down while paused, so when it resumes, it can carry on as though it still led, while another instance leads. A fencing token keeps such a leader’s late writes from overwriting the newer leader’s. Martin Kleppmann’s [How to do distributed locking](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html) explains the problem and the fix.

A _lease term_ is one unbroken stretch of leadership by one instance, from when it starts leading until it stops. Each lease term has one fencing token: `fencingToken` is the current lease term’s, or null while this instance doesn’t lead. It is the same throughout a lease term, and greater in each later lease term, whichever instance leads it. `AlwaysLeader` holds a single permanent lease, with an unlimited lease term, so its token is always 0.

The work reads the token as it starts, skips its writes if it is null, and sends it with each write:

```kotlin
  PeriodicAppService("digest", binder.config("digest.loop"), PeriodicGate.leader(leaderElection)) {
    val token = leaderElection.fencingToken ?: return@PeriodicAppService  // null: this instance doesn't lead
    val position = processNewEntries()
    cursors.advance("digest", position, token)  // false: a later lease term has written it, and this one is over
  }
```

Bootable can’t fence the writes itself: the store must be configured to refuse a write whose token is lower than the highest it has seen. Then, once a later leader has written, a paused leader’s late writes fail, rather than overwrite the newer ones. A good way to do that is to persist the token alongside the data it guards, and make each write conditional on it, with a `WHERE` clause that the writer’s token is at least the persisted one:

```kotlin
// one row for each loop, which the schema's migration inserts
object CursorTable : Table("cursor") {
  val name = varchar("name", 50)
  val position = long("position")       // the last entry the loop has processed
  val fence = long("fence").default(0)  // the highest fencing token that has written the row
  override val primaryKey = PrimaryKey(name)
}

class Cursors(private val db: Database) {
  /** Moves cursor [name] to [position], unless a later lease term has written it; returns whether it did. */
  suspend fun advance(name: String, position: Long, token: Long): Boolean = db.withTransaction {
    val updated = CursorTable.update({ (CursorTable.name eq name) and (CursorTable.fence lessEq token) }) {
      it[CursorTable.position] = position
      it[CursorTable.fence] = token
    }
    updated == 1
  }
}
```

That is, in SQL, `UPDATE cursor SET position = :position, fence = :token WHERE name = :name AND fence ⇐ :token`; when it updates no row, a later leader has written it, and this lease term is over. Each write persists its own token as it succeeds, so the fence only rises. Persist the token in each row the work updates, as here, or in a single row that holds the highest token, updated with the same `WHERE` clause in the same transaction as the work’s writes, rolling the transaction back if it updates no row.

### Kubernetes’s lease terms

`KubernetesLeaderElection`'s lease term is one pod’s unbroken hold of the Lease, and its token is the Lease’s `spec.leaseTransitions`, as of the write that started the lease term. A new lease term increments it: when another pod takes the Lease, and when a pod that stepped down takes it again, even if the Lease still names it, since its earlier lease term’s work might still be running. Renewals leave it as it is.

The tokens increase because the Kubernetes API server, backed by etcd, orders the writes that start lease terms, rather than the pods do. Every write to the Lease is conditional on the `resourceVersion` the pod read, a compare-and-set that etcd applies atomically: a write based on an outdated read fails with a 409 Conflict. So a pod can start a lease term only by writing `leaseTransitions + 1` over the latest Lease, and of two pods that race to take it, one write succeeds and the other must read the Lease again. Each lease term’s token is therefore one more than the previous one’s, whatever the pods' clocks say, or however long one of them pauses.

Deleting the Lease starts the count again, at 0, so a store that has seen a higher token would refuse every leader’s writes: leave the Lease in place, or reset the fences with it.

### When to lead, and when not to

Leadership is hard; use the right tool for the work at hand:

- **State in a store you own**, such as a counter, an aggregate, or a cursor of what has been processed: lead, and fence the writes with the token, as above.
- **Effects outside that store**, such as sending an email or calling a webhook: a fencing token can’t guard these, since the other system doesn’t check it. A leader that pauses mid-send leaves its successor unsure whether the send happened, so it must choose between at-least-once (retry, and maybe send twice) and at-most-once (don’t, and maybe never send). Choose at-least-once, and pass an idempotency key, such as the row’s id, for the receiver to drop duplicates: the effect then happens exactly once.
- **The intent to send, with the change that causes it**: a transactional outbox writes both in one transaction; its relay still delivers at least once, so it needs an idempotent receiver too.
- **Work spread over rows**, such as draining an outbox, or tasks: lock each row, with `SELECT …​ FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or use [db-scheduler](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/scheduler.html.md), rather than elect a leader.

Once the receiver is idempotent, a single leader is only an optimization, to avoid duplicate work.

## Wire

**Vanilla:**

Build the HTTP clients with the election’s defaults, give the election its client, gate the loops on it, and pass both to `Bootable`, since the election is a service too:

```kotlin
  val leaderConfig = binder.config<KubernetesLeaderElectionConfig>("leader.kubernetes")
  val clients = KtorClientService(
    binder.config("http.client"),
    CioClientEngine(),
    defaults = listOf(kubernetesClientDefaults(leaderConfig)),  // in a pod, the client trusts the API server
  )
  val leaderElection = KubernetesLeaderElection(leaderConfig, clients.getOrDefault(leaderConfig.httpClient))
  val periodic = PeriodicServices(PeriodicGate.leader(leaderElection))  // the loops run on the leader only

  return Bootable(
    setOf(
      clients,
      leaderElection,  // it is a service too: it takes part in the election while the application runs
      periodic.create("notifications", binder.config("notifications.loop")) { notifications.sendPending() },
    ),
  )
```

**Kodein:**

Import `kubernetesLeaderElectionModule`, which binds the `LeaderElection` and adds the election to the app-service set, after `ktorClientModule`, with an engine:

```kotlin
fun leaderDI() = DI {
  import(bootableModule)
  import(hopliteConfigModule)
  import(ktorClientModule)                   // the HTTP clients, from http.client
  bindSingleton<KtorClientEngine> { CioClientEngine() }
  import(kubernetesLeaderElectionModule)     // the LeaderElection, from leader.kubernetes, after ktorClientModule
  import(periodicModule)                     // its loops gated on that LeaderElection
  // ... and the loops
}
```

**Koin:**

Include `kubernetesLeaderElectionModule()`, which defines the `LeaderElection` and adds the election to the app services, with `ktorClientModule()` and an engine:

```kotlin
fun leaderKoin() = koinApplication {
  modules(
    bootableModule(),
    hopliteConfigModule(),
    ktorClientModule(),                // the HTTP clients, from http.client
    module { single<KtorClientEngine> { CioClientEngine() } },
    kubernetesLeaderElectionModule(),  // the LeaderElection, from leader.kubernetes, over ktorClientModule()'s clients
    periodicModule(),                  // its loops gated on that LeaderElection
    // ... and the loops
  )
}.koin
```

**Metro:**

`boot-leader-k8s-metro` contributes the `LeaderElection`, and adds the election to the app-service set; `boot-client-http-ktor-metro` contributes the clients, and needs an engine:

```kotlin
// boot-leader-k8s-metro contributes the LeaderElection, and boot-client-http-ktor-metro the HTTP clients it calls
// the API server with; the application chooses their engine.
@ContributesTo(BackgroundScope::class)
interface HttpClientEngineBindings {
  @Provides fun ktorClientEngine(): KtorClientEngine = CioClientEngine()
}
```

**Inara:**

Compose `kubernetesLeaderElectionModule()`, which provides the `LeaderElection` and marks the election `@AppServices`; it requires a `KtorClientModule`, here `ktorClientModule(…​)` with its engine:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface LeaderAppModule :
  ConfigModule, BootableModule, KtorClientModule, KubernetesLeaderElectionModule, OpenTelemetryApiModule,
  PeriodicModule {
  // ... and the loops
}

fun leaderAppModule() = LeaderAppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),
  bootableModule = bootableModule(),
  ktorClientModule = ktorClientModule(CioClientEngine()),  // the HTTP clients, from http.client, on that engine
  // the LeaderElectionModule, from leader.kubernetes; it requires the KtorClientModule, to call the API server
  kubernetesLeaderElectionModule = kubernetesLeaderElectionModule(),
  openTelemetryApiModule = NoopOpenTelemetryModule,        // required by periodicModule: no tracing of the runs
  periodicModule = periodicModule(),                       // its loops gated on that leaderElection
)
```

`periodicModule` and `boot-periodic-metro` gate the loops on the `LeaderElection` on their own. With no `LeaderElection`, as without `boot-leader-k8s`, every instance runs them.

## Reference

- [`LeaderElection`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-leader-common/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.leader/-leader-election/index.html): whether this instance leads, and its fencing token
- [`awaitLeadership`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-leader-common/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.leader/await-leadership.html): suspends until it does
- [`AlwaysLeader`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-leader-common/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.leader/-always-leader/index.html): always leads
- [`KubernetesLeaderElection`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-leader-k8s/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.leader.k8s/-kubernetes-leader-election/index.html): holds a Lease
- [`KubernetesLeaderElectionConfig`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-leader-k8s/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.leader.k8s/-kubernetes-leader-election-config/index.html): its settings
- [`kubernetesClientDefaults`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-leader-k8s/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.leader.k8s/kubernetes-client-defaults.html): its HTTP client’s defaults

# Scheduled tasks (db-scheduler)

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/scheduler.html

> db-scheduler's persistent tasks, recurring and one-time, over the application's database, run once across its instances.

`boot-scheduler-db` runs [db-scheduler](https://github.com/kagkarlsson/db-scheduler) over the application’s database, with `DbSchedulerService`. Its tasks, recurring and one-time, are kept in a table, so they survive restarts, and run once across all the application’s instances: each execution runs on whichever instance locks its row first. So, unlike a periodic loop, a task needs no leader election.

The service builds db-scheduler’s `Scheduler` over `boot-db-jdbc`'s `DataSource`, and starts and stops it with the application. It is in the `Serving` phase, after the `DbMilestones.SchemaMigrated` milestone, so it starts once its table is migrated and the services its tasks use have started, and stops before them. Creating it opens no connection.

## When to use it

Use a task for work that must happen once, at a time or on a schedule, such as a reminder an hour from now, or a nightly report, and that must not be lost when the application restarts. Use a [periodic loop](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html.md) for work that polls, such as sending what is pending: it runs in the process, needs no table, and runs on every instance, or, with its leader gate, on one.

## Tasks

The tasks are db-scheduler’s own, from `Tasks`. A recurring task is scheduled when the scheduler starts; a one-time task runs the executions the application schedules. A `DbSchedulerTaskProvider`, usually the class whose work its tasks do, provides them all, and exposes each typed, so code can schedule instances of it:

```kotlin
class Reminders(private val notifications: Notifications) : DbSchedulerTaskProvider {
  // one-time: an execution for each reminder, whose instance id is the reminder's id
  val send: OneTimeTask<Void> = Tasks.oneTime("send-reminder").execute { instance, _ ->
    runBlocking { notifications.sendReminder(instance.id) }  // db-scheduler runs tasks on threads of its own
  }

  // recurring: scheduled when the scheduler starts, then every hour
  val purge: RecurringTask<Void> = Tasks.recurring("purge-reminders", fixedDelay(1.hours)).execute { _, _ ->
    notifications.purgeSent()
  }

  override fun tasks() = listOf(send, purge)
}
```

db-scheduler runs each execution on a thread of its own, so a task calls suspending code with `runBlocking`. `fixedDelay` and `exponentialBackoff`, a failure handler, take Kotlin’s `Duration`.

### Schedule a one-time task

The `Scheduler` is a `SchedulerClient`, which schedules, reschedules, and cancels executions. `schedule`, `scheduleIfNotExists`, `reschedule`, and `scheduledTo` take Kotlin’s `Instant`:

```kotlin
class ReminderApi(
  private val reminders: Reminders,
  private val scheduler: SchedulerClient,
  private val clock: Clock = Clock.System,
) {
  /** Sends reminder [id] in an hour, from whichever instance locks its execution first. */
  fun remindInAnHour(id: String) {
    scheduler.schedule(reminders.send.instance(id), clock.now() + 1.hours)
  }
}
```

The execution is a row in the table, so it runs even if this instance stops first.

### Task data

A task’s data, of the class given to its task, such as `Tasks.oneTime("send-reminder", Reminder::class.java)`, is stored as JSON with kotlinx-serialization, by `KotlinxSerializationTaskDataSerializer`, rather than with db-scheduler’s default Java serialization. The data’s class must be `@Serializable`, and can’t be generic: wrap a `List<String>` in a class of its own. A subclass of a sealed `@Serializable` type is stored with its discriminator, and must have a `@SerialName`, so that renaming or moving it doesn’t strand the data already stored. Unknown keys are ignored, so an older instance reads data that a newer one wrote.

For a recurring task whose schedule is chosen at runtime, `Tasks.recurringWithPersistentSchedule`, a `SerializableSchedule` (`Cron`, `FixedDelay`, or `DailyAt`) is stored with the data: implement `PersistentScheduleData` in the data’s class.

## Its table

The module ships db-scheduler’s table as a Flyway migration for PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 (and MariaDB), and SQLite. Add its location to [Flyway](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/flyway.html.md)'s `locations`, alongside your own, which then need naming too:

```hocon
db {
  flyway {
    locations = ["classpath:db/migration", "classpath:bootable/db-scheduler/postgresql"]
  }
}
```

The locations are `classpath:bootable/db-scheduler/postgresql`, `…/mysql`, and `…/sqlite`. Each holds a repeatable migration, `R__bootable_db_scheduler.sql`, whose statements are all idempotent (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`), rather than a versioned one, whose version could clash with the application’s own, or be out of order in a database that already has later ones.

It creates the table as `scheduled_tasks`, db-scheduler’s default, with its `priority` column. With another `tableName`, or for another database, create the table with a migration of your own, from db-scheduler’s DDL in its repository.

Flyway reaches `DbMilestones.SchemaMigrated`, so the scheduler starts once the table exists.

## Configure

`DbSchedulerConfig` reads `db.scheduler`. Every setting is optional, and an unset one keeps db-scheduler’s default:

```hocon
db.scheduler {
  threads = 5                     (1)
  pollingStrategy = LockAndFetch  (2)
  shutdownMaxWait = 20s           (3)
}
```

- (1) Caps how many tasks execute at once on this instance, such as to leave the pool connections for the application’s requests; 10 by default.
- (2) Fetches and locks the due executions in one statement, `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, for fewer statements on PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, and the other databases that support it. `Fetch`, the default, works on every database.
- (3) Lets shutdown finish within the platform’s limit. db-scheduler’s default is 30 minutes, longer than most platforms wait for a process to stop, such as Kubernetes’s 30 second grace period: set it to fit.

The others include `pollingInterval`, 10 seconds by default, `immediateExecution`, to run an execution scheduled for now at once rather than at the next poll, `heartbeatInterval`, `missedHeartbeatsLimit`, `deleteUnresolvedAfter`, `tableName`, `schedulerName`, `priority`, `dialect`, and `persistTimestampsInUtc`: see [all the settings](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/api/boot-scheduler-db/com.github.rocketraman.bootable.scheduler.db/-db-scheduler-config/index.html). The SQL dialect, `dialect`, is `Auto` by default: from the database’s JDBC URL when the service is given it, as the DI flavours do, or else detected from the database when the scheduler starts.

For a db-scheduler setting `DbSchedulerConfig` doesn’t cover, such as a `SchedulerListener`, an `ExecutionInterceptor`, or another serializer, add a `DbSchedulerCustomizer`, which adjusts db-scheduler’s `SchedulerBuilder` after the typed settings, to its set binding, or, with vanilla wiring, pass one to `DbSchedulerService`.

## Readiness

`DbSchedulerHealthCheck` is a readiness check that the scheduler is running: started, and neither paused nor shutting down. It is opt-in, since readiness that depends on the scheduler takes the instance out of rotation when it isn’t running, which helps only when the application’s requests depend on its tasks. Add it to the checks of `HealthLifecycleController`, import `dbSchedulerHealthCheckModule` with Kodein, include `dbSchedulerHealthCheckModule()` with Koin, or name `DbSchedulerHealthCheckBindings` in the graph’s `bindingContainers` with Metro.

## Wire

**Vanilla:**

Construct the service over the pool’s `DataSource`, with the tasks, and pass it to `Bootable`, with Flyway to migrate its table:

```kotlin
  val jdbcConfig = binder.config<SqliteConfig>("db.jdbc")
  val database = JdbcDataSourceService(jdbcConfig, HikariConnectionPoolFactory(binder.config("db.pool")))
  val reminders = Reminders(Notifications())
  val scheduler = DbSchedulerService(
    database.dataSource,
    binder.config("db.scheduler"),
    reminders.tasks(),
    jdbcUrl = jdbcConfig.jdbcUrl,  // the SQL dialect, from the URL
  )
  val reminderApi = ReminderApi(reminders, scheduler.scheduler)

  return Bootable(
    setOf(
      database,
      FlywayMigrationService(database.dataSource, binder.config("db.flyway")),  // migrates the scheduler's table
      scheduler,
      // ... and the services that use reminderApi
    ),
  )
```

**Kodein:**

Import `dbSchedulerModule`, which binds the `Scheduler` and the `SchedulerClient`, and add your task providers to the `Set<DbSchedulerTaskProvider>` it opens:

```kotlin
fun schedulerDI() = DI {
  import(bootableModule)
  import(hopliteConfigModule)
  import(jdbcDataSourceModule)
  import(sqliteConfigModule)
  import(hikariPoolModule)
  import(flywayMigrationModule)  // migrates the scheduler's table
  import(dbSchedulerModule)      // the scheduler, from db.scheduler, and its SchedulerClient

  bindSingleton { new(::Notifications) }
  bindSingleton { new(::Reminders) }
  inBindSet<DbSchedulerTaskProvider> { add { singleton { instance<Reminders>() } } }
  bindSingleton { ReminderApi(instance(), instance()) }  // the Reminders, and the SchedulerClient
  // ... and the services that use ReminderApi
}
```

**Koin:**

Include `dbSchedulerModule()`, which defines the `Scheduler` and the `SchedulerClient`, and runs the tasks of every `DbSchedulerTaskProvider` definition; give each of yours a qualifier of its own:

```kotlin
fun schedulerKoin() = koinApplication {
  modules(
    bootableModule(),
    hopliteConfigModule(),
    jdbcDataSourceModule(),
    sqliteConfigModule(),
    hikariPoolModule(),
    flywayMigrationModule(),  // migrates the scheduler's table
    dbSchedulerModule(),      // the scheduler, from db.scheduler, and its SchedulerClient
    module {
      single { Notifications() }
      single { Reminders(get()) }
      single<DbSchedulerTaskProvider>(named<Reminders>()) { get<Reminders>() }
      single { ReminderApi(get(), get()) }  // the Reminders, and the SchedulerClient
      // ... and the services that use ReminderApi
    },
  )
}.koin
```

**Metro:**

`boot-scheduler-db-metro` contributes the service, the `Scheduler`, and the `SchedulerClient`, and `boot-db-flyway-metro` the migrations that create its table; contribute your task providers:

```kotlin
@ContributesTo(BackgroundScope::class)
interface ReminderBindings {
  @Provides @SingleIn(BackgroundScope::class)
  fun reminders(notifications: Notifications): Reminders = Reminders(notifications)

  @Provides @IntoSet
  fun reminderTasks(reminders: Reminders): DbSchedulerTaskProvider = reminders  // its tasks, to the scheduler

  @Provides @SingleIn(BackgroundScope::class)
  fun reminderApi(reminders: Reminders, scheduler: SchedulerClient): ReminderApi = ReminderApi(reminders, scheduler)
  // ... and the services that use ReminderApi
}
```

**Inara:**

Compose `dbSchedulerModule()`, which provides the `Scheduler` and the `SchedulerClient`, and mark your task providers `@DbSchedulerTaskProviders`:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface SchedulerAppModule :
  ConfigModule, BootableModule, JdbcDataSourceModule, HikariPoolModule, FlywayMigrationModule,
  OpenTelemetryApiModule, DbSchedulerModule {
  val notifications: Notifications
  @DbSchedulerTaskProviders val reminders: Reminders  // its tasks, to the scheduler
  val reminderApi: ReminderApi
  // ... and the services that use ReminderApi
}

fun schedulerAppModule() = SchedulerAppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),
  bootableModule = bootableModule(),
  jdbcDataSourceModule = jdbcDataSourceModule(SqliteConfigSource),
  hikariPoolModule = hikariPoolModule(),
  flywayMigrationModule = flywayMigrationModule(),   // migrates the scheduler's table
  openTelemetryApiModule = NoopOpenTelemetryModule,  // required: no tracing of the executions
  dbSchedulerModule = dbSchedulerModule(),           // the scheduler, from db.scheduler, and its schedulerClient
  notifications = Binding.single { Notifications() },
  reminders = Binding.single { Reminders(notifications) },
  reminderApi = Binding.single { ReminderApi(reminders, schedulerClient) },
)
```

## Telemetry

`boot-scheduler-db` can make each execution a trace of its own, with `dbSchedulerTracing`, a `DbSchedulerCustomizer`: a root span named for the task, such as `db-scheduler send-reminder`, so that the execution’s queries and log events belong to it. The span carries the task’s name, the instance’s id, and how many executions of it in a row failed before, as `bootable.db_scheduler.task`, `bootable.db_scheduler.instance`, and `bootable.db_scheduler.consecutive_failures`.

The span covers the execution’s completion too, such as the statement that deletes a one-time execution’s row or reschedules a recurring one. An execution that fails ends its span with an error status and the exception recorded, before db-scheduler’s failure handler reschedules it. db-scheduler’s own statements, such as its polls for due executions and its heartbeats, run outside any execution, so, with [statement tracing](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/index.html.md#telemetry), each is still a trace of its own.

It depends only on the OpenTelemetry API, through [`boot-telemetry-otel-common`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md#spans); the application’s SDK, such as [`boot-telemetry-otel`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md)'s, records the traces.

**Vanilla:**

Pass `dbSchedulerTracing` to `DbSchedulerService` as its customizer:

```kotlin
  DbSchedulerService(
    dataSource,
    binder.config("db.scheduler"),
    reminders.tasks(),
    customizer = dbSchedulerTracing(telemetry.openTelemetry),  // a trace for each execution
  )
```

**Kodein:**

`dbSchedulerModule` traces each execution whenever there is an `OpenTelemetry` binding, such as `openTelemetryModule`'s, and not at all when there is none:

```kotlin
  import(openTelemetryModule)  // dbSchedulerModule traces each execution
```

The tracing’s interceptor is outermost, before those that the `Set<DbSchedulerCustomizer>` adds.

**Koin:**

`dbSchedulerModule()` traces each execution whenever there is an `OpenTelemetry` definition, such as `openTelemetryModule()`'s, and not at all when there is none:

```kotlin
includes(openTelemetryModule())  // dbSchedulerModule() traces each execution
```

The tracing’s interceptor is outermost, before those of the `DbSchedulerCustomizer` definitions.

**Metro:**

`boot-scheduler-db-metro` traces each execution whenever the graph has an `OpenTelemetry`, such as `boot-telemetry-otel-metro`'s, and not at all when it has none: there is nothing to wire. The tracing’s interceptor is outermost, before those that the contributed customizers add.

**Inara:**

`dbSchedulerModule()` requires an `OpenTelemetryApiModule`, and traces each execution through it: compose `openTelemetryModule()` to trace, or `NoopOpenTelemetryModule` for none:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface TracedSchedulerAppModule :
  // OpenTelemetryModule in place of OpenTelemetryApiModule: it is one, with the SDK
  ConfigModule, BootableModule, JdbcDataSourceModule, HikariPoolModule, OpenTelemetryModule, DbSchedulerModule

fun tracedSchedulerAppModule() = TracedSchedulerAppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),
  bootableModule = bootableModule(),
  jdbcDataSourceModule = jdbcDataSourceModule(SqliteConfigSource),
  hikariPoolModule = hikariPoolModule(),
  openTelemetryModule = openTelemetryModule(),  // dbSchedulerModule traces each execution
  dbSchedulerModule = dbSchedulerModule(),
)
```

### Sampling, or no tracing

Each execution’s trace is sampled as the SDK’s sampler decides, such as at the configured `sampleRatio`. For tasks that run rarely enough that every execution’s trace is worth keeping, sample them all with `Sample.Always`, as [for the periodic loops](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html.md#telemetry). With Kodein or Metro, a `DbSchedulerTracingOptions` binding sets that, with Koin, a `DbSchedulerTracingOptions` definition, and with Inara, `dbSchedulerModule`'s `tracingOptions`; with `enabled = false`, it turns the tracing off:

**Vanilla:**

```kotlin
  DbSchedulerService(
    dataSource,
    binder.config("db.scheduler"),
    reminders.tasks(),
    customizer = dbSchedulerTracing(telemetry.openTelemetry, Sample.Always),
  )
```

**Kodein:**

```kotlin
  bindSingleton { DbSchedulerTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always) }  // or enabled = false, to trace no execution
```

**Koin:**

```kotlin
single { DbSchedulerTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always) }  // or enabled = false, to trace no execution
```

**Metro:**

Provide it in a binding container that the graph names:

```kotlin
@BindingContainer
object AlwaysSampledSchedulerTracing {
  @Provides fun dbSchedulerTracingOptions(): DbSchedulerTracingOptions =
    DbSchedulerTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always)  // or enabled = false
}

@DependencyGraph(
  BackgroundScope::class,
  additionalScopes = [BootScope::class],
  bindingContainers = [AlwaysSampledSchedulerTracing::class],
)
interface AlwaysSampledSchedulerGraph : BootableGraph
```

**Inara:**

The options are a parameter of the builder:

```kotlin
  // a parameter of the builder; or enabled = false, to trace no execution
  dbSchedulerModule = dbSchedulerModule(tracingOptions = DbSchedulerTracingOptions(sample = Sample.Always)),
```

The setting applies to every task.
