# Examples

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/index.html

> Runnable applications in the repository's examples directory, each showing Bootable functions put together.

Each example is a small application in the repository’s [`examples`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples) directory, built against the Bootable modules in the same repository. Run any of them from the repository root with Gradle; they are services, so they run until you stop them with Ctrl-C.

- [Wiring styles](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/wiring.html.md): the smallest application, one service that logs a greeting from config, wired five ways (vanilla, Kodein, Koin, Metro, and Inara).
- [Ktor server](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor.html.md): a Ktor server on Netty with typed config, which can also be built as a GraalVM native image; vanilla wiring.
- [Server with a database](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor-db.html.md): a key/value store over HTTP with the database, telemetry, an HTTP client, health probes, and background work, wired five ways (vanilla, Kodein, Koin, Metro, and Inara), with a container image that has a JVM AOT cache.
- [Custom start order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/start-order.html.md): a Ktor server and a ready file, with a custom lifecycle phase; vanilla wiring.
- [Web app with Compose HTML](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/compose-html.html.md): a todo list with a Compose HTML browser client and a Ktor server, sharing their models; vanilla wiring.
- [Web app with htmx](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/htmx.html.md): the same todo list, rendered on the server with kotlinx.html and made interactive with htmx; vanilla wiring.
- [Web app with Kilua](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/kilua.html.md): the same todo list with a Kilua client, rendered on the server by a Node.js process that Bootable starts before the Ktor server; vanilla wiring.

`examples/di-bench` is not an example of Bootable: it is a benchmark of how long Kodein, Koin, and Metro take to build graphs of 25, 100, and 400 services, and doesn’t use Bootable.

---

# Wiring styles

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/wiring.html

> The smallest Bootable application, one service that logs a greeting, wired with plain Kotlin, Kodein, Koin, Metro, and Inara.

Five examples, `wiring-vanilla`, `wiring-kodein`, `wiring-koin`, `wiring-metro`, and `wiring-inara`, are the same application, wired each of the five ways Bootable supports. The application is one `AppService`, `GreetingService`, which logs a message from config as it starts. Comparing them shows what each wiring style asks of an application, with nothing else in the way; [Choosing a wiring style](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md) says how to choose between them.

> **Note:** Kodein is deprecated, as its authors are sunsetting it: for a new application, consider Inara, its compile-time successor, or Koin, for a DSL like Kodein’s.

## What it uses

- `boot`, the lifecycle, which runs the service and stops it on a signal.
- `boot-config-hoplite`, for the `greeting` config section; see [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md).
- `boot-logging-log4j2`, for the log; see [Logging (Log4j2)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md).

The Kodein, Koin, Metro, and Inara examples use the `-kodein`, `-koin`, `-metro`, and `-inara` flavours of `boot` and `boot-config-hoplite`; the Inara example applies KSP, with Inara’s processor.

Each reads the same config, from `src/main/resources/application.conf`:

```hocon
greeting { message = "hello from Bootable" }
```

## Wire

**Vanilla:**

Load the config, construct the service, and hand it to `Bootable`:

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  val binder = hopliteConfigBinder()
  Bootable(
    appServices = setOf(GreetingService(binder.config("greeting"))),
  )
}
```

**Kodein:**

Import Bootable’s and the config binder’s modules, bind the config and the service, and resolve the `Bootable`:

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  val di = DI {
    import(bootableModule)
    import(hopliteConfigModule)
    bindConfig<GreetingConfig>("greeting")
    bindAppService { singleton { GreetingService(instance()) } }
  }
  di.direct.instance<Bootable>()
}
```

**Koin:**

Include Bootable’s and the config binder’s modules, define the config, and the service with a qualifier of its own, and resolve the `Bootable`:

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  koinApplication {
    modules(
      bootableModule(),
      hopliteConfigModule(),
      module {
        config<GreetingConfig>("greeting")
        single<AppService>(named("greeting")) { GreetingService(get()) }
      },
    )
  }.koin.get<Bootable>()
}
```

**Metro:**

Contribute the service into the set of services, provide its config, and let the compiler build the graph:

```kotlin
sealed interface AppScope

@ContributesIntoSet(AppScope::class)
@SingleIn(AppScope::class)
@Inject
class GreetingService(private val cfg: GreetingConfig) : AppService {
  private val log = logger()
  override suspend fun start() = log.info { "greeting: ${cfg.message}" }
}

@ContributesTo(AppScope::class)
interface AppConfigBindings : ConfigBinderProvider {
  @Provides fun greetingConfig(): GreetingConfig = config("greeting")
}

@DependencyGraph(AppScope::class, additionalScopes = [BootScope::class])
interface AppGraph : BootableGraph

fun main() = boot {
  createGraph<AppGraph>().bootable
}
```

**Inara:**

Compose the config’s and Bootable’s modules with the application’s own members, mark the service `@AppServices`, and let KSP generate the module’s builder, which takes a binding for each member:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface AppModule : ConfigModule, BootableModule {
  val greetingConfig: GreetingConfig
  @AppServices val greetingService: GreetingService
}

fun main() = boot {
  AppModule(
    configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),
    bootableModule = bootableModule(),
    greetingConfig = config("greeting"),
    greetingService = Binding.single { GreetingService(greetingConfig) },
  ).bootable
}
```

Leaving out a binding fails the compilation.

In the vanilla, Kodein, and Koin examples, `GreetingService` is a plain class, with no annotations.

## Run it

From the repository root:

**Vanilla:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-vanilla:run
```

**Kodein:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-kodein:run
```

**Koin:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-koin:run
```

**Metro:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-metro:run
```

**Inara:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:wiring-inara:run
```

The log shows the start plan, then the greeting:

```kotlin
Start plan: Application[GreetingService]
greeting: hello from Bootable
```

The application has no server, so there is nothing to open; it runs until you stop it with Ctrl-C. Change the message with the environment, as `GREETING_MESSAGE=hi ./gradlew :examples:wiring-vanilla:run`.

## Source

- [`examples/wiring-vanilla`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/wiring-vanilla)
- [`examples/wiring-kodein`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/wiring-kodein)
- [`examples/wiring-koin`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/wiring-koin)
- [`examples/wiring-metro`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/wiring-metro)

# Ktor server

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor.html

> A small Ktor server on Netty, with typed config, run by Bootable and buildable as a GraalVM native image.

`server-ktor` is a Ktor server with three routes, wired with plain Kotlin and run by Bootable. It shows the least an HTTP application needs: a `KtorService` with its own routes, typed config for it, and logging. It is also the repository’s GraalVM native-image smoke test, relying only on the native-image metadata bundled in the Bootable jars.

## What it uses

- `boot-server-http-ktor-netty`, for `NettyKtorService`, the server on Ktor’s Netty engine; see [Server (Ktor)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md).
- `boot-config-hoplite`, for the `server` and `hello` config sections; see [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md).
- `boot-logging-log4j2`, for the log; see [Logging (Log4j2)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md).

The server is an ordinary class, constructed in `main`:

```kotlin
class ExampleServer(config: ServerConfig, private val hello: HelloConfig) : NettyKtorService("test", config) {
  override fun Application.module() {
    routing {
      get("/hello") { call.respond(HttpStatusCode.OK, hello.response) }
      // ...
    }
  }
}

fun main() = boot {
  val binder = hopliteConfigBinder()
  Bootable(
    appServices = setOf(
      ExampleServer(binder.config("server"), binder.config("hello")),
    )
  )
}
```

`ServerConfig` implements `HostPort`, which is how a `KtorService` finds the address to listen on, from `server.host-port` in `src/main/resources/application.conf`.

## Run it

From the repository root:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor:run
```

It serves [http://localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000):

- `/` is an HTML index, with links to the other two routes.
- `/hello` answers with `hello.response` from the config, `world!`.
- `/die` answers, then fails the server’s scope: Bootable logs that the service failed, stops every service, and exits with status 1.

## Build a native image

The project applies GraalVM’s native build plugin, so with a GraalVM JDK, `nativeCompile` builds an executable:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor:nativeCompile
examples/server-ktor/build/native/nativeCompile/server-ktor
```

The build fails on a missing reflection or resource registration, rather than falling back to the JVM, so a clean run, and a clean shutdown on SIGTERM, shows the bundled metadata is enough.

## Source

[`examples/server-ktor`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/server-ktor)

---

# Server with a database

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor-db.html

> A key/value store over HTTP, with a database, telemetry, an HTTP client, health probes, and background work, wired five ways.

`server-ktor-db` is a Ktor server that stores named entries in a SQLite database, and traces and measures itself with OpenTelemetry. Its `GET /relay/{name}` calls the server back through a lifecycle-managed Ktor `HttpClient`, as a call to another service would be made. In the background, a periodic loop logs the entry count, on the leader only, and a db-scheduler task logs a digest of the entries.

It is the example that puts most of Bootable’s functions together, and it is wired each of the five ways: the server, repository, table, migrations, and config are shared, in `common`, and `vanilla`, `kodein`, `koin`, `metro`, and `inara` are each a runnable application. `jib` builds the vanilla application into a container image, with its JVM AOT cache in it.

## What it uses

- [Database](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/index.html.md): SQLite ([`boot-db-jdbc-sqlite`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/drivers.html.md)) through a HikariCP pool ([`boot-db-pool-hikari-otel`](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/hikari.html.md)), migrated by [Flyway](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/flyway.html.md), and queried with [Exposed](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/exposed.html.md), which verifies the `entry` table against the migrated schema; `boot-db-jdbc-otel` traces each query.
- [HTTP server](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md): `EntryServer`, a `CioKtorService`, on Ktor’s CIO engine.
- [HTTP client](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/client.html.md): the named client `entries`, from `boot-client-http-ktor-cio`, traced by `boot-client-http-ktor-otel`.
- [Health](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md): liveness and readiness, served by the server as JSON, with readiness down while the database doesn’t answer, and the [build info](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md#build-info).
- [Telemetry](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md): the OpenTelemetry SDK, a Prometheus scrape at `/metrics`, the server’s request traces and metrics, the pool’s metrics, and a trace of the application’s start, with a span for each service’s start.
- [Periodic work](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html.md): the entry count’s loop, gated on [leader election](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md) through a Kubernetes Lease, which the config skips outside Kubernetes (`leader.kubernetes.assumeLeader = true`).
- [Scheduled tasks](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/scheduler.html.md): the entry digest, a recurring db-scheduler task, whose table Flyway migrates with the application’s.
- [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md) and [Logging](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md), as in every example.

`SeedEntriesService` stores two sample entries on a first run. It starts after the `DbMilestones.SchemaMigrated` milestone, in the `Initialization` phase, so it runs on a migrated schema, and before the server takes a request.

## Wire

**Vanilla:**

`EntriesApp`, in `vanilla/src/main/kotlin/App.kt`, constructs every service and lifecycle controller in plain Kotlin, and `main` hands them to `Bootable`:

```kotlin
fun main() = boot {
  val app = EntriesApp(hopliteConfigBinder())
  Bootable(app.services, app.lifecycleControllers)
}
```

The order of the set doesn’t matter: each service declares where it starts, and Bootable logs the start plan.

**Kodein:**

`appDI()`, in `kodein/src/main/kotlin/App.kt`, imports each module’s Kodein module, and `entriesModule`, the application’s own bindings:

```kotlin
fun appDI() = DI {
  import(bootableModule)
  import(hopliteConfigModule)
  import(openTelemetryModule)
  // ... telemetry, server, health, and client modules
  import(jdbcDataSourceModule)
  import(sqliteConfigModule)
  import(hikariPoolModule)
  import(flywayMigrationModule)
  import(exposedDatabaseModule)
  // ... leader election, periodic, and db-scheduler modules
  import(entriesModule)
}

fun main() = boot {
  appDI().direct.instance<Bootable>()
}
```

**Koin:**

`appKoin()`, in `koin/src/main/kotlin/App.kt`, includes each module’s Koin module, and `entriesModule`, the application’s own definitions, each with a qualifier of its own where it adds to the app services or the tables:

```kotlin
fun appKoin(): KoinApplication = koinApplication {
  modules(
    bootableModule(),
    hopliteConfigModule(),
    openTelemetryModule(),
    // ... telemetry, server, health, and client modules
    jdbcDataSourceModule(),
    sqliteConfigModule(),
    hikariPoolModule(),
    flywayMigrationModule(),
    exposedDatabaseModule(),
    // ... leader election, periodic, and db-scheduler modules
    entriesModule,
  )
}

fun main() = boot {
  appKoin().koin.get<Bootable>()
}
```

**Metro:**

The `-metro` modules contribute their bindings on their own; `EntriesBindings`, in `metro/src/main/kotlin/App.kt`, contributes the application’s, and the graph adds two binding containers:

```kotlin
@DependencyGraph(
  AppScope::class,
  additionalScopes = [BootScope::class],
  bindingContainers = [ServiceStartTracingBindings::class, JdbcHealthCheckBindings::class],
)
interface AppGraph : BootableGraph

fun main() = boot {
  createGraph<AppGraph>().bootable
}
```

Leaving out the driver or the pool fails the compilation with a missing binding.

**Inara:**

`EntriesModule`, in `inara/src/main/kotlin/App.kt`, is the application’s own module, which requires the Bootable modules it uses; `AppModule` composes it with them, each once:

```kotlin
@DIModule(composed = true)
interface AppModule :
  ConfigModule, BootableModule, OpenTelemetryModule,
  // ... telemetry, server, health, and client modules
  JdbcDataSourceModule, HikariPoolModule, FlywayMigrationModule, ExposedDatabaseModule,
  // ... leader election, periodic, and db-scheduler modules
  EntriesModule

fun appModule(): AppModule = AppModule(
  configModule = hopliteConfigModule(),
  bootableModule = bootableModule(),
  openTelemetryModule = openTelemetryModule(),
  // ...
  jdbcDataSourceModule = jdbcDataSourceModule(SqliteConfigSource),
  hikariPoolModule = hikariPoolModule(),
  flywayMigrationModule = flywayMigrationModule(),
  exposedDatabaseModule = exposedDatabaseModule(setOf(EntryTable)),
  // ...
  entriesModule = entriesModule(),
)

fun main() = boot {
  appModule().bootable
}
```

Leaving out the driver or the pool, or any module another requires, fails the compilation.

## Run it

From the repository root:

**Vanilla:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:vanilla:run
```

**Kodein:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:kodein:run
```

**Koin:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:koin:run
```

**Metro:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:metro:run
```

**Inara:**

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:inara:run
```

Each serves [http://localhost:8001](http://localhost:8001), and keeps its database in its own directory, at `build/entries.db`. The config is in `common/src/main/resources/application.conf`.

## Endpoints

[http://localhost:8001](http://localhost:8001) is an index page, with a form to try each operation, the API, and the entries stored so far.

**`GET /entries`**

Lists every entry, one `name=value` per line.

**`GET /entries/{name}`**

Returns an entry’s value, or 404.

**`PUT /entries/{name}`**

Stores the request body as the entry’s value.

**`DELETE /entries/{name}`**

Removes an entry, or answers 404.

**`GET /relay/{name}`**

Gets an entry by calling `GET /entries/{name}` on this server through the `entries` HTTP client, configured under `http.client.named.entries`.

**`GET /metrics`**

The Prometheus scrape.

**`GET /health/live`**

Liveness: 200 until the application has stopped.

**`GET /health/ready`**

Readiness: 200 while the application is running and the database answers, 503 otherwise.

**`GET /health/info`**

The build info, from the `build` config section.

For example, store an entry, and get it back through the HTTP client:

```shell
curl -X PUT --data 'hello' http://localhost:8001/entries/greeting
curl http://localhost:8001/relay/greeting
```

The health endpoints answer in JSON, with the lifecycle state, and readiness with its one check, the database’s, by name:

```shell
$ curl -s http://localhost:8001/health/live
{"status":"UP","state":"Running"}
$ curl -s http://localhost:8001/health/ready
{"status":"UP","state":"Running","checks":{"jdbc":{"status":"UP"}}}
```

So a script can check the database:

```shell
curl -s http://localhost:8001/health/ready | jq -e '.checks.jdbc.status == "UP"'
```

To see readiness go down before the server stops, set a drain delay, as `HEALTH_READINESS_DRAINDELAY=10s`, stop the application with Ctrl-C, and ask for readiness during the delay.

Start the application with a version, such as `BUILD_VERSION=1.4.2`, and a test can check which build answered it:

```shell
curl -s http://localhost:8001/health/info | jq -e '.version == "1.4.2"'
```

## Metrics and traces

As configured, the example has no OTLP endpoint, so it pushes nothing: its metrics are only pulled, from its Prometheus scrape, which needs nothing else running. After a few requests, the scrape has the server’s request metrics, the pool’s, the JVM’s, and the example’s own counter, `entries_stored_total`:

```shell
curl -s http://localhost:8001/metrics | grep -E 'entries_stored|http_server_request_duration_seconds_count|db_client_connections_usage'
```

Traces are only pushed, so they need a collector, and an OTLP endpoint to reach it. With one set, the example pushes its metrics there too, every `metrics.interval`, and still serves the scrape. Grafana’s `otel-lgtm` image runs a collector, with Tempo, Prometheus, Loki, and Grafana, in a single container:

```shell
podman run --rm -p 3000:3000 -p 4318:4318 docker.io/grafana/otel-lgtm
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4318 TELEMETRY_SDK_METRICS_INTERVAL=5s ./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:vanilla:run
```

In Grafana, at [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000), search Tempo for the service `entries`. Each request is a trace, with a span for the database operation, such as `entries.put`, and a span for each of its queries within that. `GET /relay/{name}` has a client span, with the server’s own `GET /entries/{name}` within it, since the client carries the trace in a `traceparent` header. The application’s start is a trace too, `start application`, with a span for each service’s start.

Jaeger takes OTLP as well: run `docker.io/jaegertracing/jaeger:latest` with ports 16686 and 4318, and open [http://localhost:16686](http://localhost:16686).

Log lines written within a request carry its `trace_id` and `span_id`.

## Start faster, with an AOT cache

The `vanilla` application has an `aotCache` task, which runs the installed application once, serving a few requests, to write its JVM AOT cache; run the application with it:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:vanilla:aotCache
cd examples/server-ktor-db/vanilla
JAVA_OPTS=-XX:AOTCache=build/aot/vanilla.aot build/install/vanilla/bin/vanilla
```

The `jib` project builds the vanilla application into a container image, `bootable-examples/server-ktor-db-jib`, with the cache in it. The JVM only uses a cache with the same JDK build and the same jars as the run that trained it, so the training runs in a container of the image itself, and the final image adds the cache as one more layer:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:jib:jibDockerBuild -PcontainerCli=podman
podman run --rm -p 8001:8001 bootable-examples/server-ktor-db-jib
```

Leave out `-PcontainerCli=podman` to use Docker. The repository’s `server-ktor-db` [Dagger](https://dagger.io) module builds the same image as a CI pipeline. `mise run demo` uses it to run the image with the `otel-lgtm` stack, in containers, with the OTLP endpoint set, so its traces and metrics are pushed to Grafana at [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000).

See [Faster start: the JVM AOT cache](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/aot-cache.html.md) for how the cache is trained, and what it gains.

## Tests

```shell
./gradlew :examples:server-ktor-db:common:test :examples:server-ktor-db:vanilla:test :examples:server-ktor-db:kodein:test :examples:server-ktor-db:koin:test :examples:server-ktor-db:metro:test
```

`common` tests the routes against a real SQLite database, and each application tests its own wiring.

## Source

[`examples/server-ktor-db`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/server-ktor-db)

# Custom start order

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/start-order.html

> A Ktor server and a ready file, ordered with a custom lifecycle phase.

`start-order` is a Ktor server that writes a _ready file_ once it is listening, and removes it before it stops. A ready file exists only while the application takes traffic, so something outside the process, such as a Kubernetes `exec` readiness probe or a supervisor, can tell when to send requests.

It shows how an application adds a phase to Bootable’s start order. Bootable’s default phases end with `Serving`, the server’s, and the ready file must be written after it. So the application adds a phase, `Announce`, after the default ones:

```kotlin
enum class AppPhase : Phase { Announce }

object AppStartOrder : StartOrder by DefaultStartOrder {
  override val phases = DefaultStartOrder.phases + AppPhase.Announce
}
```

`ReadyFileService` declares `Ordering(AppPhase.Announce)`, and `main` passes `startOrder = AppStartOrder` to `Bootable`. Shutdown runs the plan in reverse, so the ready file is removed while the server still answers. Without `AppStartOrder`, the boot fails before any service starts, because `Announce` is not one of the default phases. See [Start order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md) for how the start order works.

## What it uses

- `boot`, for the start order: `StartOrder`, `DefaultStartOrder`, `Phase`, and `Ordering`.
- `boot-server-http-ktor-cio`, for `CioKtorService`, the server on Ktor’s CIO engine; see [Server (Ktor)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md).
- `boot-config-hoplite`, for the `server` and `ready-file` config sections; see [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md).
- `boot-logging-log4j2`, for the log; see [Logging (Log4j2)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md).

It is wired with plain Kotlin.

## Run it

From the repository root:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:start-order:run
```

Bootable logs the plan before anything starts:

```kotlin
Start plan: Serving[HelloServer] Announce[ReadyFileService]
```

While it runs, [http://localhost:8005](http://localhost:8005) answers, and the ready file, `examples/start-order/build/ready`, exists. Stop it with Ctrl-C, and the log shows the file removed before the server stops.

## Source

[`examples/start-order`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/start-order)

---

# Web app with Compose HTML

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/compose-html.html

> A todo list in Kotlin end to end, with a Compose HTML browser client and a Ktor server run by Bootable.

`compose-html` is the same todo list as [htmx](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/htmx.html.md) and [Kilua](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/kilua.html.md), written in Kotlin end to end: a browser client written with [Compose HTML](https://github.com/JetBrains/compose-multiplatform#compose-html), and a Ktor server run by Bootable. The server serves the client’s files and a JSON API, so the whole application runs as one process and one jar.

It is in three projects:

**`shared`**

The API’s models (`Todo`, `NewTodo`, `TodoUpdate`), its path, and the rule for a valid title, in a Kotlin Multiplatform module compiled for the browser and the JVM, so the client and the server agree on the JSON and on what makes a todo valid.

**`client`**

The Compose HTML UI, compiled to JavaScript, which calls the API with Ktor’s client, and checks a title with the shared rule as the user types.

**`server`**

`TodoServer`, a `NettyKtorService`, which serves the JSON API under `/api/todos`, and the client’s files at `/`, and checks every title with the same shared rule.

Todos are kept in memory; [Server with a database](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor-db.html.md) stores data in a database.

The same application is also written with [htmx](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/htmx.html.md), rendered on the server, and with [Kilua](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/kilua.html.md), rendered on the server and then in the browser.

## What it uses

- `boot-server-http-ktor-netty`, for the server on Ktor’s Netty engine; see [Server (Ktor)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md).
- `boot-config-hoplite`, for the `server` config section; see [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md).
- `boot-logging-log4j2`, for the log; see [Logging (Log4j2)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md).

The server is the only service, wired with plain Kotlin:

```kotlin
fun appServices(binder: ConfigBinder): Set<AppService> = setOf(
  TodoServer(binder.config("server"), TodoRepository()),
)

fun main() = boot {
  Bootable(appServices = appServices(hopliteConfigBinder()))
}
```

## Run it

From the repository root:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:compose-html:server:run
```

Then open [http://localhost:8002](http://localhost:8002).

The server’s build copies the client’s production bundle onto its classpath, under `web/`, so this one command builds the client too. The server’s jar and distribution (`installDist`, `distZip`) contain the client, and need nothing else to run.

### Live reload

For changes to the UI, run the client from Kotlin/JS’s webpack development server, which reloads the page whenever the client is rebuilt. Run the server in one terminal, for the API, and the development server in another:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:compose-html:server:run
./gradlew --continuous :examples:compose-html:client:jsBrowserDevelopmentRun
```

Then open [http://localhost:8080](http://localhost:8080), webpack’s port, which forwards requests under `/api` to the server. Changes to `client` or `shared` are picked up without a restart; changes to `server` still need one.

## Tests

```shell
./gradlew :examples:compose-html:server:test
```

The tests run the server’s routes in Ktor’s test host, with a client that sends and receives the shared models, and check that the server serves the client’s bundle.

## Source

[`examples/compose-html`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/compose-html); its README also covers styling a Compose HTML application.

---

# Web app with htmx

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/htmx.html

> A todo list rendered on the server with kotlinx.html, and made interactive with htmx, by a Ktor server run by Bootable.

`htmx` is the same todo list as [Compose HTML](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/compose-html.html.md) and [Kilua](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/kilua.html.md), rendered on the server with [kotlinx.html](https://github.com/kotlin/kotlinx.html), and made interactive with [htmx](https://htmx.org/).

`GET /` returns the whole page, already rendered, so the browser shows the todos before any script runs. The page’s elements carry htmx attributes, such as `hx-post`, `hx-patch`, and `hx-delete`, which htmx turns into requests; the server answers each with a fragment of HTML, which htmx swaps into the page. The page and the fragments are rendered by the same functions, in `Views.kt`, so the first render and later updates can’t disagree.

The server serves htmx’s script itself, at `/assets/htmx.min.js`, taken from htmx’s webjar by the build, so the application needs no CDN. Todos are kept in memory; [Server with a database](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor-db.html.md) stores data in a database.

## What it uses

- `boot-server-http-ktor-netty`, for `TodoServer`, a `NettyKtorService`; see [Server (Ktor)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md).
- `boot-config-hoplite`, for the `server` config section; see [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md).
- `boot-logging-log4j2`, for the log; see [Logging (Log4j2)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md).
- Ktor’s `ktor-server-htmx` and `ktor-htmx-html`, for the `hx { }` route scope and typed `hx-*` attributes.

The server is the only service, wired with plain Kotlin, as in [Compose HTML](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/compose-html.html.md).

## Run it

From the repository root:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:htmx:run
```

Then open [http://localhost:8003](http://localhost:8003).

The routes the page calls, each answering with a fragment:

**`POST /todos`**

Adds a todo, returning its item, or, for a title that isn’t valid, a 422 with the form and the reason.

**`PATCH /todos/{id}`**

Marks a todo done or not, returning its item, or 404.

**`DELETE /todos/{id}`**

Removes a todo, or 404.

Parts of the page that a change affects elsewhere, such as the count of todos done, come in the same response, marked `hx-swap-oob`, and htmx swaps them in by id.

## Tests

```shell
./gradlew :examples:htmx:test
```

The tests make requests as htmx does, in Ktor’s test host, and check the full page, the fragments, the refusals, and that htmx’s script is served.

## Source

[`examples/htmx`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/htmx); its README compares it with compose-html.

---

# Web app with Kilua

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/kilua.html

> A todo list with a Kilua client, rendered on the server by a Node.js process that Bootable starts before the Ktor server.

`kilua` is the same todo list as [Compose HTML](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/compose-html.html.md) and [htmx](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/htmx.html.md), written with [Kilua](https://kilua.dev), a web framework built on JetBrains' Compose runtime. The client runs in the browser, as in compose-html, but with server-side rendering, so each page arrives with its content, as in htmx.

Kilua renders on the server by running the client itself, in Node.js. It shows how Bootable runs a process that the server depends on: `SsrRenderer`, an `AppService`, starts the renderer, and the server, in a later phase, starts only once it is up.

It is in three projects, as compose-html is: `shared`, the models and the title rule; `client`, the Kilua UI, bundled for the browser and, as `ssr.zip`, for Node.js; and `server`, which serves the rendered page at `/`, the client’s files, and the JSON API under `/api/todos`. Todos are kept in memory; [Server with a database](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/examples/server-ktor-db.html.md) stores data in a database.

## What it uses

- `boot`, for the order of the two services: `SsrRenderer` declares no phase, so it is in `Application`, and `TodoServer`, as a `KtorService`, is in `Serving`, which starts after it and stops before it.
- `boot-server-http-ktor-netty`, for `TodoServer`, a `NettyKtorService`; see [Server (Ktor)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md).
- `boot-config-hoplite`, for the `server` and `ssr` config sections; see [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md).
- `boot-logging-log4j2`, for the log; see [Logging (Log4j2)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md).

The two services are wired with plain Kotlin, in `server/src/main/kotlin/App.kt`:

```kotlin
fun appServices(binder: ConfigBinder): Set<AppService> {
  val serverConfig = binder.config<ServerConfig>("server")
  val renderer = SsrRenderer(binder.config("ssr"), serverConfig.localUrl())
  return setOf(
    renderer,
    TodoServer(serverConfig, TodoRepository(), renderer),
  )
}
```

`SsrRenderer.start()` starts Kilua’s `SsrEngine`, which runs the renderer in Node.js, and returns once the renderer has rendered a first page, so the server never takes a request it can’t render. It has no `shutdown()`: `SsrEngine` stops Node.js only from a JVM shutdown hook, after Bootable has stopped the server.

## Run it

The server needs Java 25, since Kilua’s `kilua-ssr-server` is built for it, and Node.js; `run` uses the Node.js that the Kotlin Gradle plugin downloads. From the repository root:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:kilua:server:run
```

Then open [http://localhost:8004](http://localhost:8004). To see what server-side rendering adds, look at the first response, before any script runs:

```shell
curl http://localhost:8004/
```

The log shows the renderer start before the server, and stop after it.

Run from the server’s jar or distribution, it runs `node` from the `PATH`; set `SSR_NODE` to use another.

### Live reload

As in compose-html, run the server in one terminal, and the client’s development server in another:

```shell
./gradlew :examples:kilua:server:run
./gradlew --continuous :examples:kilua:client:jsBrowserDevelopmentRun
```

Then open [http://localhost:8080](http://localhost:8080), which forwards requests under `/api` to the server. Pages aren’t rendered on the server this way: the client loads the todos and renders them in the browser.

## Tests

```shell
./gradlew :examples:kilua:server:test
```

`TodoServerTest` runs the API in Ktor’s test host. `ServerRenderingTest` starts the renderer and the server in Bootable’s order, and checks that the first response is the rendered page, with the latest todos; without Node.js it is skipped, except on CI.

## Source

[`examples/kilua`](https://github.com/rocketraman/bootable/tree/master/examples/kilua); its README explains the rendering in detail, and compares the three todo list examples.

---

# Bootable and Spring Boot

Source: https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/comparison/spring-boot.html

> Why you might use Bootable rather than Spring Boot, when Spring Boot is the better choice, and how Spring Boot's concepts map onto Bootable's.

Spring Boot is the best-known way to boot and run a server-side application on the JVM, so the first question about Bootable is usually: why not Spring Boot? At root, both start an application, configure it, run it, and stop it cleanly. They differ in how much magic and runtime discovery they use, how complex they are, and in how much of the system is explicit vs hidden behind abstractions.

## Then and now

Spring began, in 2003, as the lightweight alternative to the application servers of the day: Enterprise JavaBeans, vendor-specific deployment, and the ceremony that came with them. Dan Tanner’s article, [Spring Rites](https://dantanner.com/post/spring-rites/), lists some of the real problems it solved then, such as configuring an application, avoiding lock-in to an application server vendor, and unit testing. As he argues, those problems are either irrelevant today, or made worse by Spring Boot. In many ways, Spring has become the heavyweight it once displaced.

Spring is an annotation-based framework that hides vast swathes of functionality behind those easy annotations. As Tanner argues, these make code harder to reason about and harder to test, maintain, and extend than their plain Kotlin counterparts.

## Explicit, not discovered

Spring Boot discovers the application at runtime. It scans the classpath for annotated components, and its auto-configuration adds beans for whatever libraries it finds there, unless a condition says otherwise. Annotations then change what the code does: `@Transactional` makes a method transactional through a proxy, and `@Scheduled` runs it on a timer. This is easy to start with, but not simple: what runs, and why, is decided by rules outside your code, and a mistake can do nothing at all, silently, such as `@Transactional` on a `private` method, which the proxy never sees.

Even deciding what a "bean" is and "configuration" is difficult to understand. `@Component`, `@Service`, and `@RestController` make a class a bean, but only if a `@ComponentScan` finds it. `@Configuration` classes declare beans with `@Bean` methods, but the same method on a plain `@Component` is something different. `@AutoConfiguration` classes add beans for you, but complicates this with all sorts of conditions: `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, and so on. Just importing a dependency changes your application in ways that it is impossible to understand. Easy, but definitely not simple. `@Profile`, `@Primary`, `@Qualifier`, and `@Lazy` change which of multiple beans is chosen, and when it is created. `@ConfigurationProperties` binds config, but only once something enables it, and `@ConstructorBinding` decides whether it binds through the constructor or through setters, a rule that changed between Spring Boot 2 and 3. `@Configurable` even injects into objects created with `new`, through AspectJ weaving. Which beans exist, and which one is injected where, is the sum of all of these, at runtime, and often visible only in the conditions report, or the debugger.

Bootable runs what your `main` gives it. There is no scanning, no auto-configuration, and no annotation that changes behaviour; a module does nothing until you wire it. The application is two sets, its services and its lifecycle controllers, which you build by hand, or with a DI container such as Kodein, Koin, Metro, or Inara. With Metro, the graph is checked at compile time, so a missing binding is a build error rather than a failed start. See [No magic](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/philosophy.html.md).

## The libraries, used directly

Spring Boot tends to put its own abstractions in front of the libraries it uses: Spring Data in front of the database, Spring MVC or WebFlux in front of the server, Spring Messaging in front of Kafka, and its own configuration model in front of each library’s. You then need to understand both the library **and** Spring’s abstraction of it, and many of the underlying library’s capabilities are hard or impossible to reach through that abstraction.

Bootable integrates libraries chosen for server-side Kotlin, and exposes them rather than wrapping them: Ktor for HTTP, Exposed, HikariCP, and Flyway for databases, Hoplite for configuration, db-scheduler for persistent tasks, and the OpenTelemetry SDK for telemetry. An optional module sets up the common case and exposes the library’s own types. Where a module doesn’t fit, leave it out, and integrate the library, or another one, yourself.

## A lifecycle you can read

Startup ordering not expressed inherently via dependencies are managed via `SmartLifecycle` beans and phase numbers, `@DependsOn`, or an `@Order` value relative to everyone else’s. Spring introduced order coupling in annotations, in order to avoid it in code. But annotations are code, and the coupling introduced is real.

Bootable [starts services](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md) in named phases and milestones so there is no coupling via global ordering. A test can check the plan, under many orders of the services left unordered, without starting anything. See [Lifecycle and services](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html.md) and [Start order](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md).

## Testing without booting

Spring Boot’s `@SpringBootTest` starts the application context in a test, and slices such as `@WebMvcTest` start part of it. These offer easy shortcuts, but a suite written that way tends to become full of mocks, slow to run, and brittle as the application evolves. Programmers used to these shortcuts cease to think about class abstractions, and start to assume the dependencies available in production are the same dependencies available in test — bringing back the very problems that early DI frameworks like Spring were trying to solve!

Bootable deliberately has no built-in way to boot the application in a test. It is easy enough to do yourself if you really need it, but treat it as a code smell, except for very specialized use cases. Instead, follow classic coding rules: think about class dependencies and abstractions, architect code to make it unit testable, and construct a class with fakes for what it uses, and check the wiring and the start plan without starting anything. See [Testing](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/testing/index.html.md).

## Startup and footprint

With no scanning, no reflection-driven configuration, and no proxies, a Bootable application adds almost no overhead to startup or the runtime.

Each of Spring’s layers is in the call stack too: its proxies, interceptors, filter chains, and dispatchers, for transactions, security, and the rest of what its annotations auto-magically add. A stack trace from a Spring Boot application is often mostly Spring’s frames, before it reaches the application’s own classes, which adds overhead, makes it harder to understand runtime behavior, and makes debugging more complex.

Bootable adds no proxies and no interceptors, and isn’t in the path of a request at all.

## When Spring Boot is the better choice

The usual reasons to choose Spring Boot mostly come down to familiarity, and familiarity has costs of its own.

**"Its ecosystem integrates everything: Spring Security, Spring Data, Spring Integration, Spring Cloud."**

The libraries underneath already offer abstractions, designed by the people who know them best. The Spring layer on top costs you in cognitive load and in the capabilities available to you, and adds runtime overhead. The old case for that layer was swapping one technology for another. An application that keeps each library behind a port of its own, isolated and tested, can swap it without a framework’s help, and, with an AI’s help, in a fraction of the time it once took.

**"Our team already knows Spring."**

That is a real cost of switching, and worth weighing. But much of knowing Spring well is knowing its rules and workarounds, while knowing the language and the libraries directly is more useful fundamental knowledge.

**"Spring has a large community, extensive documentation, and commercial support."**

Spring’s community is well earned: it pioneered ideas, such as dependency injection, that every framework now takes for granted. But its documentation is extensive because Spring is large and complex. Bootable is small enough to read in an afternoon, or for an AI to hold in a single conversation and answer from, and a framework you can understand is one you need little support for.

**"Our application is in Java, and will stay that way."**

Then Spring Boot, or another Java framework, is the better choice: Bootable, and Ktor and Exposed beneath it, are written for Kotlin.

## From Spring Boot to Bootable

For a reader who knows Spring Boot, the nearest equivalent of each of its concepts:

| Spring Boot | Bootable |
| --- | --- |
| `SpringApplication.run`, from `main` | `boot { }`, whose block returns the `Bootable` to run; see [the application](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html.md#boot). |
| Component scanning, `@Component`, and `@Bean` | No scanning: construct the services, or bind them in Kodein, Koin, Metro, or Inara; see [Choosing a wiring style](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/wiring.html.md). |
| Auto-configuration and starters | A module per integration, each wired explicitly; see [All modules](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/modules.html.md). |
| `SmartLifecycle` and `ApplicationRunner` | `AppService`, whose `start` and `shutdown` Bootable calls; see [services](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/lifecycle.html.md#services). |
| `SmartLifecycle` phases and `@DependsOn` | [Phases](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md#phases) and [milestones](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/concepts/start-order.html.md#milestones). |
| `application.yml` and `@ConfigurationProperties` | HOCON, decoded by Hoplite into typed config classes; see [Configuration](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/configuration/index.html.md). |
| Profiles, such as `application-prod.yml` | The deployment environment, from config, and no implicit per-environment files; see [Environment](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/environment/index.html.md). |
| Logback | Log4j2; see [Logging (Log4j2)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/logging/index.html.md). |
| `DataSource` auto-configuration, with HikariCP | A driver module and `boot-db-pool-hikari`; see [Database](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/index.html.md). |
| Flyway auto-configuration | `boot-db-flyway`; see [Migrations (Flyway)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/flyway.html.md). |
| Spring Data JPA or JDBC | Exposed; see [ORM (Exposed)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/database/exposed.html.md). |
| Spring MVC or WebFlux | A Ktor server; see [Server (Ktor)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/server.html.md). |
| `RestClient` or `WebClient` | Ktor `HttpClient`s; see [Client (Ktor)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/client.html.md). |
| Actuator’s health, liveness, and readiness | `HealthLifecycleController`, served over HTTP by `KtorHealth`; see [Health](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/http/health.html.md). |
| `@Scheduled` | A periodic loop; see [Periodic work](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/periodic.html.md). |
| Quartz | db-scheduler’s persistent tasks; see [Scheduled tasks (db-scheduler)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/scheduler.html.md). |
| Spring Cloud Kubernetes leader election | `boot-leader-k8s`; see [Leader election](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/background/leader.html.md). |
| Micrometer and Micrometer Tracing | The OpenTelemetry SDK, used directly; see [Telemetry (OpenTelemetry)](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/telemetry/index.html.md). |
| `@SpringBootTest` | None, by design: test classes with fakes, and check the wiring and start plan; see [Testing](https://rocketraman.github.io/bootable/bootable/next/testing/index.html.md). |
